Then the Almighty says:

﴿That was Our argument, which We gave to Abraham against his people. We raise by degrees whom We will. Indeed your Lord is Wise and All-Knowing.﴾ (6:83)

The argument (ḥujja, a decisive proof established to demonstrate the matter under claim) is the sound proof set up to establish the thesis that is sought to be proven. It is as though the Almighty, exalted is He, wants us, when we debate, to have an aim in the debate. We know that if the aim of debate goes beyond the subject of the debate, whether to negate or to affirm, it becomes mere clamour, and the matter is confined to your wanting to defeat your opponent while your opponent tries to defeat you. Rather, when you enter into debate, you must make the original aim the foundation, as they say: defining and clarifying the point of dispute. For the truth must be dearer to you and to your opponent than either of you. This is why we find that the Almighty explains: beware of disputing a matter in a public contest. Why? Because in a public clamour truth gets mixed up with falsehood, and God, glorified is He, wants every voice to be attributed to its owner. For example, when a great demonstration takes place and someone's downfall is chanted, no one knows who started the chant.

What caused the Arabs to lose was that when they received the call, they were thinking in terms of public gatherings, in which they criticised the sayings of the Messenger of God, and so they lost the capacity for objective judgement.

This is why our Lord says:

﴿Say: I only advise you of one thing: that you stand up for God, in pairs and individually, and then reflect. There is no madness in your companion.﴾ (34:46)

That is, that you should gather with God as your direction. Whoever has the strength should debate the sayings of the Messenger of God by argument, in subject matter, history and logic. Two people cannot come together to examine a question while God alone is in their minds without reaching a unified opinion on it. This is why secret negotiation in the modern age has derived from that faith-based principle.

﴿That was Our argument, which We gave to Abraham against his people. We raise by degrees whom We will. Indeed your Lord is Wise and All-Knowing.﴾ (6:83)

The first of Abraham's people was his father Azar. He argued with them about the stars, the moon, the sun and the idols. After that he prevailed by argument over their chief, who was the king or sultan, namely Nimrod, when he wanted to debate with him about the power to give life and cause death.

The Truth wants us to learn from the wisdom of our master Abraham: when you see your opponent entering into matters in which the dispute can never end, move him to the level from which he cannot escape or get free, so that he does not overcome you. The king Nimrod said to him:

﴿I give life and cause death.﴾ (2:258)

Abraham could have said: "You do not cause death, you kill, and killing is not dying, because you destroy the structure." But he did not want to prolong the dispute. He wanted the debate to be concise, to drop him onto the argument and bind him by it by the shortest path. So God said:

﴿Abraham said: Indeed God brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west.﴾ (2:158)

So what was the outcome of the debate? God, glorified is He, says:

﴿So the one who disbelieved was confounded.﴾ (2:158)

All these are arguments that the saying of God, glorified is He, explains:

﴿That was Our argument, which We gave to Abraham against his people. We raise by degrees whom We will. Indeed your Lord is Wise and All-Knowing.﴾ (6:83)

God, glorified is He, gave Abraham the argument against his people, meaning that he had over them degrees, eminence and elevation. For establishing the argument against another is a victory, and victory is a raising of the rank of your subject and also a raising of the subject of your work. God, glorified is He, wills only with wisdom and wills only with knowledge, because if we were to let the will of one of mankind go unrestricted, he might act without wisdom and without knowledge. But the Truth informs us that His will is with wisdom and knowledge for the benefit of creation, because His will is founded not on whim, nor on benefit from anyone. God, glorified is He, possesses all the attributes of perfection, majesty and beauty before He created creation.

The creation of creatures and their faith add nothing to God's dominion, and if they disobey, nothing is subtracted from God's dominion. But wisdom may escape some of the creatures, so they do not perceive it. When God, glorified and exalted is He, decrees a matter upon His creatures and they accept it even though they do not know its reason, He shows them the wisdom in the act that had been unacceptable to them. This is because He created the creatures and knows from eternity that creatures have desires and wishes, and if He gave every creature its wish, He would give it at the expense of others. The Almighty is just, so He does not benefit one and afflict another.

By His wisdom the Truth knows what sets right the affairs of His creation, so He does not respond to a foolish request from a servant. God knows that it is not in the servant's interest that He fulfil this request for him. This is why the Truth says:

﴿And man prays for evil as he prays for good, and man is ever hasty.﴾ (17:11)

A servant says: "O Lord, do this for me, ease this matter for me," and it is good in his view, though it may be evil, because man is hasty. Therefore He, glorified is He, says:

﴿I will show you My signs, so do not seek to hasten them.﴾ (21:37)

The Truth, majestic and exalted is He, regulates the wishes of creation, so He carries out for them what is beneficial.

﴿We raise by degrees whom We will. Indeed your Lord is Wise and All-Knowing.﴾ When the word "Lord" (rabb) occurs, we must understand from it the meaning of creation and nurture, whereas when the word "divinity" (ilāhiyya, the state of being the one worshipped and obeyed) appears, let us know that it is for the purpose of being subject to commands. For God is the one worshipped and obeyed, whether He commands or forbids. But the Lord is the one who created, nurtured, took charge of you, and gave you the means of your life. So the gift of lordship (rubūbiyya) is one thing, and the gift of divinity (ulūhiyya) is another. The gift of lordship is received by believer and disbeliever, obedient and disobedient, because God is the One who brought them into existence and made the universe subservient to them. But the gift of divinity is embodied in "do this" and "do not do that", and this falls within the realm of choice. So whoever disbelieves in God and skilfully takes the means receives their results, while whoever believes in God but does not skilfully take the means does not receive the results, because drawing out what is in the universe is part of the gift of lordship.

The Truth (Allah) says:

﴿And We bestowed upon him Isaac and Jacob, each of whom We guided. And Noah We guided before, and of his descendants David, Solomon, Job, Joseph, Moses and Aaron. Thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾

We know that Isaac is the second son of our master Ibrahim (Abraham), after Isma'il (Ishmael), and Ya'qub (Jacob) is the son of Isaac. When you see the word "gift" (hibah), understand that it is not "the truth" (al-haqq). A gift is one thing, and "the truth" (al-haqq) is another thing. The gift is the giving of a giver to one who does not deserve it, because when you give a person what he deserves, that is not a gift but a right (haqq).

And the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted is He, makes clear: Beware lest you believe that any of My creatures has a right over Me, except what I make a right for him. Rather, everything is a gift from Me. The first summit of gifts and bestowals is the first lordship in the universe given to man, then multiplication through the two kinds of male and female, where offspring are sons and daughters. He, glory be to Him, says:

﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He creates what He wills. He bestows females upon whom He wills, and He bestows males upon whom He wills.﴾ (Surat ash-Shura, 49)

So the gift of children does not come merely from the fact that He created the man and the woman, and that their union produces children. Rather, He, glory be to Him, says:

﴿Or He gives them both males and females, and He makes whomever He wills barren.﴾ (part of verse 50 of Surat ash-Shura)

If the matter were merely a mechanical process, children would come. But the matter is not so. Whoever understands the dominion (malakut) finds his soul at peace, knowing that this occurs through the wisdom of the All-Wise, who knows that it is a gift from Allah. Even barrenness is a gift. Whoever receives it from Allah as a gift and is content with it, and does not look upon the children of others with envy or jealousy, Allah will make everyone you see into your children without the hardship of carrying or giving birth, and without any care or nurture from you throughout your life. And whoever is content with Allah's gift of daughters will find that they are a provision from Allah, and He will raise up for him sons who will marry and daughters who will be more obedient to him than his sons, because he is content. Therefore one must accept the gift both in giving and in withholding.

The Truth makes clear: I gave Ibrahim Isaac, and after Isaac, Ya'qub. Each of us knows that man, by the reality of the decrees of the universe, is certainly going to die, and when a man grows old he desires a son whose name will continue in life, as though he has secured himself within that. If a grandson comes, the grandfather has secured for himself another generation. But let us know the saying of the Truth:

﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world, but the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord in reward and better in hope.﴾ (Surat al-Kahf, 46)

And the remembrance of a man in this world has no necessity if Allah diminishes his rank in the Hereafter!!

We also note that the Truth said in another place:

﴿So grant me from Yourself an heir, who will inherit from me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub, and make him, my Lord, pleasing.﴾ (verses 5 and 6 of Surat Maryam)

Allah bestowed His favour upon Ibrahim not only through Isaac but also through Ya'qub. And beyond that He said: ﴿each of whom We guided﴾, meaning that both of them were among the people of guidance. ﴿And Noah We guided before﴾, meaning that guidance does not begin with Isaac and Ya'qub, but with Noah before them. ﴿And of his descendants David, Solomon, Job, Joseph, Moses and Aaron. Thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾

Continuing, the Truth (al-Haqq) says:

﴿And Zakariyya, Yahya, 'Isa and Ilyas; all of them were among the righteous (al-salihin)﴾ (6:85).

The Truth did not mention the eighteen prophets in one unbroken sequence; rather, He divided them with wisdom. So He says:

﴿And Isma'il, al-Yasa', Yunus and Lut; and each of them We preferred over the worlds﴾ (6:86).

A repeated text, because it shares wording with verse 85. Al-Haqq continues:

﴿And Zakariyya and Yahya and 'Isa and Ilyas, each of them among the righteous (85)﴾.

Al-Haqq did not mention the eighteen prophets in one unbroken sequence, but divided them with wisdom, so He says:

﴿And Isma'il and al-Yasa' and Yunus and Lut, and each We preferred over the worlds (86)﴾.

The matter is not limited to these, but He, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And [some] of their fathers, their descendants and their brothers. We chose them and guided them to a straight path (87)﴾.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 6, verse 87:

If you look at these eighteen prophets mentioned here, you will find that they are among the twenty-five messengers whom we are commanded to believe in individually. They have been gathered in the verse of the poet (al-Nazim):

"In that is our proof: of them eight,
after ten, and seven remain, and they are:
Idris, Hud, Shu'ayb, Salih, and likewise
Dhu al-Kifl, Adam, al-Mukhtar, and with them they conclude."

Allah, glorified and exalted, did not make any of the prophets kings except two: Dawud and Sulayman. This is to give us the idea that when Allah wishes to subdue a people to something that no one can resist, He sends a messenger who is a king, because a king cannot be overcome by a servant, since power is with him. Society at that time was in need of a king who would manage its affairs and regulate its condition. Yet He, glorified is He, does not want faith through force, fear and dread; He wants it through free choice. For this reason, most of the prophets were not kings.

There is a hadith: "Would you prefer to be a king-prophet, or a servant-messenger?" (1) So he chose to be a servant-messenger, because a king comes with his authority and his wealth, and may become tyrannical.

Allah willed that Sulayman and Dawud be among the prophets while being kings, and in them appear power, breadth of dominion and authority. As for Ayyub, he took another angle among the angles, namely trial and patience alongside prophethood. Every prophet has a shared portion of prophethood and a personal distinctiveness. Likewise Yusuf took trial first, then took kingship and authority in the end. Musa and Harun took the fame of followers, and we hardly know of religions except Judaism and Christianity. As for Zakariyya, Yahya, Isa and Ilyas, they took the quality of asceticism.

As for Isma'il, al-Yasa', Yunus and Lut, they took what their lives were filled with of great deeds, noble qualities, upright conduct and good example, and a good remembrance remained for them.

Thus there are multiple angles for the prophets.

When the scholars paused at ("Isa"), asking whether he is included in their progeny, some of them inferred and said: he is from their progeny through the mother's side. Indeed, the mothers of a people are vessels, and lineages are traced through fathers, and the human element in Isa is the mother.

By this same reasoning Abu Ja'far Muhammad al-Baqir argued before al-Hajjaj when the latter said to him: "You claim that you are the family of the Messenger of Allah and his descendants, although the Messenger of Allah has no offspring!"

Imam al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with him, said to him: "It seems you have not read the Qur'an."

He said: "And what is in the Qur'an?"

He said: "Read: ﴿And of his offspring…﴾ until you reach: ﴿and Isa﴾. So is Isa from the offspring of Nuh, through a father or through a mother?"

He said: "Through a mother." Then he said to him: "So we too are from the offspring of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 6, verse 88:

The Truth (al-Haqq) says after that:

﴿That is the guidance of Allah; He guides with it whomever He wills of His servants. And if they had associated others with Him, whatever they used to do would have been nullified for them.﴾

(That) is a reference to something mentioned earlier, and what is intended is the guidance with which We guided that people, which is the guidance of Allah. We find that the word (hudan, guidance) denotes the goal toward which a short path is laid out that leads to it. Our Lord is the One who created, the One who sets the goal, and who sets out, clarifies and makes clear the path to the goal. When guidance is attributed to Allah, it indicates the source and origin, i.e., guidance from Allah. The word (hudan) is sometimes attributed to the Giver, who is the Truth, and sometimes attributed to the prophets.

The Truth says: ﴿So follow their guidance﴾, and (that) is a reference to the method that Allah sent down to the messengers.

Thus, Allah the Glorified and Exalted guides all people by indicating to them what is good, and whoever responds to this indication, out of respect for his faith, Allah assists him and increases him in guidance. He, glory be to Him, wishes to establish for the human being that He has made him free to choose. If you choose anything, you have not chosen it against the will of our Lord; rather, you chose it by the One who created you free to choose. Nothing occurs in the universe contrary to the will of Allah. Had Allah willed all people to be guided, not one of them would have been able to disobey; but He willed them to be free to choose, and every act that any one of them performs is willed by Allah, yet it may be a will that is not loved. For this reason the scholars said: there is a will of cosmic decree (irada kawniyya) and a will of legislation (irada shar'iyya). As long as a thing is in Allah's dominion, it is willed by Allah; the legislative will is what is commanded, and whatever differs from that is the cosmic will, which comes from the fact that He created you free to choose.

An example of this, and to Allah belongs the highest likeness: you give your son a pound, and the pound has purchasing power. He takes the pound and goes out to the market, free to spend it. You say to him: listen. If you buy with it a Qur'an or a beautiful book or some sweets and eat them with your siblings, I will be pleased with you and will reward you with a good reward. But if you buy (a deck of) cards or spend the pound on what I do not approve of, I will be angry with you and will not give you money.

By this saying you have given your son freedom. When he goes to the market and buys a deck of cards, he has not done that against your will, because you are the one who gave him the choice; but you told him that you ask him to choose well. Allah the Glorified and Exalted has made the human being free to choose: if he chooses guidance, He bestows abundant giving upon him, and if he chooses misguidance, He holds him accountable for it.

As for the prophets, guidance came to them from Allah as an indication to them, and they turned toward the wills of the Truth, so He gave them another guidance: He makes them love the work and makes the doing of good beloved to them. After that, Allah, glory be to Him, makes clear: beware lest you think that anyone escapes from Me, for if they associated others with Him, their deeds would be nullified.

Thus the Truth did not create creation compelled to perform obedience; rather He created them free to choose in the obligations, so that they may attain the pleasure of choosing the method of Allah. And if they had associated, their deed would have been nullified. The "law" (law) is a particle of conditional negation for the negation of the consequent, and this is evidence that they did not associate, and therefore their deed was not nullified. (Al-habt) is the invalidation of the deed.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 6, verse 89:

﴿Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book, the judgment (ḥukm), and prophethood. If these disbelieve in them, then We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them.﴾

Al-Kitāb is the method (manhaj), and al-ḥukm is what Allah gave some of them of authority and dominance, and al-nubuwwah (prophethood); that is, He made them behavioural models for mankind.

﴿If these disbelieve in them, then We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them﴾. Glorified and exalted is He, Who gave us models of the guided ones among the messengers and the prophets, and among those whom He chose from their fathers, their offspring and their brothers. These are the people whom you came to take by the hand from darknesses into light. If some people refrain from guidance, Allah will entrust others to carry the methods, so that they may be the enduring element of goodness until the Hour comes.

And who are the people? Some of them said: the one referred to is the Quraysh, and what is meant by His words ﴿then We have entrusted them to a people who are not disbelievers in them﴾ is the people of Madinah, that is, the Anṣār. Or what is meant by the noble text is every one who refuses and disbelieves, and likewise every one who turns to Allah and obeys Him; that is, if a group disbelieves in them, Allah entrusts whoever will uphold them, defend them and protect them, because Allah does not send down a cause of goodness among creation and then obliterate it afterward; rather He must preserve it as a proof against creation.

﴿If these disbelieve in them, then We have entrusted them to a people﴾. This indicates that the people of goodness are always Allah's deputies, because whoever extends his hand with help to a weak one of Allah's creatures—this weak one has been summoned by Allah into existence—and whoever extends his hand with help has made himself a deputy of our Lord, because he performs what is required of Him, glorified is He, and has made himself a means to Him, since Allah is the Lord of all, the Educator of all, the Guardian of all, and the Provider of all. Let whoever does good and makes himself a deputy of Allah trust that Allah in spreading goodness among His creation will honour him many times over what he gave.

Then the Truth (Allah) says, after that:

﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance. Say: "I do not ask you any wage for it. It is only a reminder to the worlds."﴾ (6:90)

Here too, "guided by Allah" (hudā Allāh) is the guidance of indication (hidāyat dalāla) and the guidance of help (hidāyat ma'ūna), as evidenced by His saying: ﴿so follow their guidance﴾. The address is to our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because "those" (ulā'ika), i.e., those referred to, are the earlier ones, and the kāf (the "-ka" ending) is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance.﴾ When we recite this noble verse, we say "iqtadi" (اقتد) and not "iqtadih" (اقتده). The hā' is only pronounced in pause, and they call it (hā' al-sakt, the hā' of pausing); but when it comes in connection (waṣl), it is not pronounced. Each one of these messengers previously mentioned has a distinctive quality by which he was characterized, and there is a common element among all of them, which is sincerity of worship to Allah, faith in Allah, and that He is One in His essence, in His attributes, and in His acts. All of them share these foundations, and each one was distinguished by a quality of goodness: our master Solomon and David received power, authority and kingship; Job received the capacity for patience under trial; Joseph received the capacity for patience and excellence in judgment; our master Jonah received the capacity of one who turns humbly to Allah while he was in the belly of the fish; and Ishmael was true to his promise.

So what is required of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is that he be an imitator of all of them, that is, that he be like Solomon, like David, like Isaac, like Jacob, like Job, like Joseph, and like Jonah, and that he take from each of them the quality of distinction, and that he share with them in the general matter, which is the Oneness of Allah. Thereby all the distinction that is in all the prophets gathers in our master Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is commanded with a command from his Lord, we must believe that he (ﷺ) carried out the command. And since the excellences of the prophets have gathered in him (ﷺ), it is right for him to be the Seal of the Prophets and Messengers.

﴿Say: I do not ask you any wage for it. It is only a reminder to the worlds.﴾ (part of 6:90)

And why would one ask for a wage? You do not ask a wage from someone for whom you did a deed, unless the deed you did gives him a benefit that deserves to be paid for and rewarded with a wage. It is as if what the Prophet (ﷺ) delivers to the community deserved a wage; but he (ﷺ) conveys from his Lord: "Say to them: indeed you have dispensed with this wage."

Compare someone who provides you with a benefit that may not take half an hour of his time in some detail of life's affairs, with someone who performs a deed that benefits you in a scope that extends beyond this world to reach the Hereafter, and then says: "I do not want a wage from you."

The not seeking of a wage occurred from all the messengers except two; it is not mentioned in the Qur'an that they said it. If you look at Surah al-Shu'ara', for example, you find that the Truth speaks about Moses, and speaks about Abraham, and then speaks after that about the rest of the messengers, and the word "wage" does not appear in the story of Abraham nor likewise in the story of Moses, peace be upon them both; but mention of the wage came in other than them. He, glorified is He, says:

﴿When their brother Noah said to them: "Will you not fear Allah? Indeed I am a trustworthy messenger to you. So fear Allah and obey me. And I do not ask you any wage for it; my wage is only from the Lord of the worlds."﴾ (26:106–109)

And He, majestic is His glory, said:

﴿When Shu'ayb said to them: "Will you not fear Allah? Indeed I am a trustworthy messenger to you. So fear Allah and obey me. And I do not ask you any wage for it; my wage is only from the Lord of the worlds."﴾ (26:177–180)

When you survey Surah al-Shu'ara', you find all the prophets, and with the saying of each of them ﴿And I do not ask you any wage for it﴾, except our master Moses and our master Abraham. Why? We say: whoever renounces a wage is one who provides them a benefit.

As for Moses, peace be upon him, we find that the benefit was directed, offered and conveyed to him from Pharaoh, who raised him, as if he had taken the wage in advance. Therefore Moses did not say to Pharaoh, "I do not ask you a wage," because the Qur'an brought Pharaoh's saying:

﴿He said: Did we not raise you among us as a child?﴾ (26:18)

Likewise the matter of the wage does not appear in the story of our master Abraham, because he addressed his father Azar, and it was not acceptable for him to say to him, "I do not ask you a wage." Thus the matter of the wage was obliterated in the story of our master Abraham and the story of our master Moses, and it remained in what was other than them, which indicates that the Qur'an is composed in its most precise details with wisdom, because the one who speaks is our Lord. Our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), is also distinguished in saying: "I do not ask you a wage," except in one verse in which he made an exception to this negation:

﴿Say: I do not ask you any wage for it, except the love of kinship.﴾ (42:23)

Love (mawadda) is the doing of good arising from love of the heart; but the doing of good that does not spring from love in the heart is merely kindness (ma'ruf), because kindness a person gives to both those he loves and those he does not love. Therefore our Lord said:

﴿But if they strive with you to make you associate with Me what you have no knowledge of, do not obey them, and keep them company in this world with kindness.﴾ (31:15)

So kindness is a deed whose extension is superficial good. As for the Messenger, when he asks for love in kinship, is it the kinship of the Prophet (ﷺ) or love in your kinship? It is kinship in its absolute sense, and it is also the kinship of the speaker, who is the Messenger conveying from Allah.

If it is classified as "except the love of kinship," meaning the kinship of the speaker, who is our master the Messenger of Allah, then we could not repay him with a wage. Or, when each one of us bears a sphere of goodness and kindness among his people, here the circles of goodness among all people are interlocked.

The Truth concludes the verse by saying: ﴿It is only a reminder to the worlds﴾, which gives us the gathering of the circles; each one becomes concerned with his relatives, people compete and vie for love of kinship, and each of them is keen to widen the circle of kinship. Here goodness spreads and affection endures.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 6, verse 91:

Then the Truth (al-Haqq) says:

﴿They did not measure God with His true measure when they said, "God has not sent down anything to a human being." Say: "Who sent down the Book which Moses brought, a light and guidance for mankind, which you make into scattered pages, showing some and concealing much? And you were taught what neither you nor your fathers knew." Say: "God." Then leave them in their idle talk, playing.﴾ (91)

The discussion concerns those who rejected and refused to believe in God. The Messenger, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, is commanded to clarify to them that they did not obey God with His true measure. Qadr means knowing the measure (miqdar). The true measure of Him, glory be to Him, is beyond our capacity as humans to attain, so we measure Him according to our capacity or according to what He has asked of us. As the Messenger of God said: "Glory be to You, we cannot count the praise of You; You are as You have praised Yourself" (1).

When one of us praises someone, this is evidence that he has assessed that person's worth by the measure of the praise. When we assess the measure of God, we must know that all perfect attributes belong to Him, and they are endless and cannot be counted. Among the mercy of the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted is that He has taken upon Himself the wording of praise of Him, so that He does not put us in difficulty. No human being has the power to encompass the beauty or majesty of God so as to praise Him with what He deserves; and even if a servant could encompass it (and he will not), from where would he get the expression that conveys this praise? No eloquent person or man of letters can embellish phrases sufficient to express this praise of God. So the Truth clarified to us through His Messenger: "I have borne this matter on your behalf so that you are all equal." The Messenger of God said: "Glory be to You, we cannot count the praise of You; You are as You have praised Yourself."

In the phrase "al-hamdu lillah" alone, all people are equal. Among His mercy, glory be to Him, is that He made people equal in knowing the wording of praise of Him. The Truth here comes at the angle in which He negated that they had not measured God with His true measure. Why, O Lord, did they not measure You with Your true measure? The answer comes:

﴿when they said, "God has not sent down anything to a human being"﴾ (part of verse 91, Surat al-An'am).

That is, they denied that God would choose from among His creation someone to make them fit to receive His method and convey it to His creatures. The Truth responds to His Messenger in reply to them:

﴿Say: "Who sent down the Book which Moses brought, a light and guidance for mankind"﴾ (part of verse 91, Surat al-An'am).

So those who say this must necessarily believe that a Book was sent down to Moses, so that the argument is in its proper place. The pagans of Mecca were not believers in any messenger, but they knew that there were among the People of the Book, as shown by their saying:

﴿If only the Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than they﴾ (part of verse 157, Surat al-An'am).

We say: if you examine the surah closely, the matter may apply to one specific person among those whom the argument overpowered. In the history of the biography (sirah) we find one of the rabbis who was constantly engaged in disputing about Islam, and his name was Malik ibn al-Sayf. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, met him. The rabbi (hibr) is the scholar of the Jews, and it is presumed of him that he be among those who renounce worldly things, devoted to knowledge; yet he was fat, although it is the custom of those devoted to worship and knowledge to take from food only what sustains them and sets their backs straight, for it has come in the Torah: "Indeed God hates the fat rabbi."

When the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, learned that Malik ibn al-Sayf, who was one of the rabbis of the Jews, was engaging much in disputing Islam, he said to him: "In your Torah is there not: 'Indeed God hates the fat rabbi'?" The man was dumbfounded, and said: "God has not sent down anything to a human being" — meaning, God has not sent down anything to a human being of the sort that you are saying. Thus we learn that such a statement may come from the People of the Book. When Malik made this utterance, men of the Jews stood against him and said to him: "How can you say: 'God has not sent down anything to a human being'?" He said to them: "Muhammad angered me, so I answered anger with falsehood."

Here those Jews who heard him said: "Then you are not fit to be a rabbi, for you have disgraced us," and they removed him and brought Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and appointed him in his place.

﴿Say: "Who sent down the Book which Moses brought, a light and guidance for mankind, which you make into scattered pages, showing some and concealing much? And you were taught what neither you nor your fathers knew." Say: "God." Then leave them in their idle talk, playing.﴾ (part of verse 91, Surat al-An'am).

The Book, then, is the Book that God sent down to Moses, which is the Torah, and they have made it into scattered pages, or pages separated, showing from them what they wish and concealing from them what they do not wish, as they did in the matter of stoning as punishment for adultery. Thus concealment of what God sent down to them had already occurred, and the Truth has made this clear in several verses:

﴿But they forgot a portion of what they had been reminded of﴾ (part of verse 14, Surat al-Ma'idah).

What they did not forget, they concealed in part and revealed in part, and what they did not conceal they distorted and twisted with their tongues. So there is forgetting, concealment, and distortion. Yet they did not limit themselves to this and stop there; rather they brought things of their own and said they were from God:

﴿Woe to those who write the Book with their own hands and then say, "This is from God," to exchange it for a small price﴾ (part of verse 79, Surat al-Baqarah).

The Truth, glory be to Him, continues:

﴿And you were taught what neither you nor your fathers knew. Say: "God." Then leave them in their idle talk, playing.﴾ (part of verse 91, Surat al-An'am).

If the speech concerns the pagans of Mecca, then the Qur'an came to them with what neither they nor their fathers knew, because Islam came after a gap between the messengers. If it concerns the People of the Book, then it is a true statement, because when they concealed things, the Qur'an exposed what they concealed and what they distorted. The Qur'an came and set things right for them; it is as if they knew the truth, so that they might abrogate with it the falsehood they had altered and distorted. His saying, the Truth: ﴿Say: "God."﴾ means that the One who sent down the Book is God.

When the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, uses an interrogative form, we know that a genuine question with respect to God is impossible, because He knows everything. Rather He uses a question called the "denunciatory interrogative" (al-istifham al-inkari) or the "assertive interrogative" (al-istifham al-taqriri), and He comes with this form because He wants an answer from the obstinate that includes acknowledgment. If they do not say it, and they are perplexed or ashamed to say it, then say to them yourself, O Muhammad:

﴿Say: "God." Then leave them in their idle talk, playing.﴾ (part of verse 91, Surat al-An'am).

Al-khawd (immersion) is entering deep water in which the eye cannot discern the place of the foot, and it may descend into a pit; then it was used and borrowed for plunging into falsehood.

The Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, says: ﴿Then leave them in their idle talk, playing.﴾ That is, this is their play, and they will not be able to stand against the call; the call is proceeding on its path, and they will never prevail over it. Everything they do is immersion in falsehood and play with no benefit and no connection to seriousness. But does this mean that Muhammad should leave them? No, because whenever he finds ears among them he admonishes and reminds them; then, after the matter is established for Islam, whoever dwells in the Arabian Peninsula will accept from him only Islam or the sword, because the miracle came directly in a Qur'an whose inimitability all know, and He, glory be to Him, had previously sent down the Torah and sent down the Qur'an as a blessed Book.

1 Narrated by Muslim in the Prayer, Abu Dawud in the Prayer and Witr, al-Nasa'i in the Night Prayer, al-Tirmidhi in the Supplications, Ibn Majah in Supplication, and Malik in the Muwatta' in the chapter on touching the Qur'an; and Ahmad in the Musnad, 1/96, 118.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 6, verse 92:

Then the Truth (al-Haqq) says after that:

﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed, confirming what was before it, that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it. And those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it, and they are over their prayers, guarding them.﴾ (6:92)

The word (anzalna, "We sent down") is originally from the root n-z-l, and it is used in several ways with respect to the Qur'an. Sometimes He, glorified is He, says:

﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree.﴾ (97:1) (Surah al-Qadr)

Another time He, mighty and majestic, says:

﴿And We have sent it down in parts (nazzalnahu tanzilan).﴾ (part of 17:106) (Surah al-Isra')

Another time He attributes the descent to the Qur'an itself:

﴿And with the truth We sent it down, and with the truth it descended.﴾ (part of 17:105) (Surah al-Isra')

And another time He attributes it to the one who brought it:

﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down.﴾ (26:193) (Surah al-Shu'ara')

These, then, are various expressions. What is the reason for this variation in derivation, when we know that the Qur'an was not sent down all at once upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but rather was sent down all at once to the lowest heaven from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), so that the Qur'an might begin its mission in the new existence, and each star of the stars would descend according to events? Here (anzala) is causative (lil-ta'diya), meaning it was conveyed from the Preserved Tablet to the lowest heaven so that it might begin its mission, and for this reason He, glorified is He, says: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree.﴾

We know that the Qur'an descended on the Night of Decree and on other than the Night of Decree, but it descended in its entirety on the Night of Decree to the lowest heaven, then it descended in installments and in detail during the remaining twenty-three years that the Prophet (ﷺ) lived after the revelation began. So when He wants to say that He sent it down from the Preserved Tablet, He uses the (hamzat al-ta'diya, the causative alif), and when He wants descent and continuity, He says (nazala), because in it there is sequence (al-tatabu'). And when He attributes it to the one who brought it down, He uses (nazala), because the Qur'an did not descend alone but the Trustworthy Spirit descended with it. So all of them converge on the fact that the Qur'an was sent down (nazala), or was caused to descend (anzala), or descended (nazala). The word (nazala) gives us a hint: that it came from above, and the lower receives it. And when the Truth asks us to listen to the sending down of a ruling, He, mighty and majestic, says:

﴿Say: Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden you.﴾ (part of 6:151)

The meaning of (ta'alaw, "come") is "rise up," because we live on the earth, and beware lest the earth legislate for you, for the legislation of the earth, if it is not in the light of God's method, is abasement (hadid). God wants elevated legislation, and you must receive your rulings from heaven, so that you do not wander and do not go astray in the falsehood of legislations that do not revolve within the framework of God's method.

And the Truth says here: ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed﴾, and this statement applies to the Qur'an alone, although all the previous heavenly books were books of method, and the miracle was separate from the method. The miracle of Moses (peace be upon him), as we know, was the staff, and his method was the Torah. The miracle of Jesus (peace be upon him) was healing the blind and the leper and raising the dead by God's permission, and his method was the Gospel. But the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was distinguished in that his miracle is the very same as his method, because every religion of the earlier religions was for a limited time, in a limited place. He (ﷺ) brought the comprehensive and all-encompassing religion, therefore the miracle came to be the method. Had the miracle of the Messenger (ﷺ) been of the kind of the miracles of the earlier ones, that is, cosmic and visible, it would have ended. We did not believe in the miracles of the earlier prophets except because the Qur'an related them and they became information, each of which suits a limited time and a limited place. But Islam came to encompass all times and all places, and therefore the miracle had to accompany the method, so that whoever comes after the age of prophethood until the Hour may say: Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, this is his miracle.

The Qur'an is blessed. In our customs, when we speak in colloquial Arabic, we use a word that is from the breath and sprinkling (nafh wa nadh) of the eloquent usages we have heard, and we find someone saying: "By God, this food has baraka; it was prepared for two and four ate of it, and it overflowed and increased." So, (al-baraka) is that a thing gives more than its visible size.

The baraka of the Qur'an is dominant and overriding. If every person measured the size of the Qur'an against the size of other books, he would find the Qur'an's size smaller, yet it contains such goodness, righteousness, blessings, legislations, miracles and secrets that books are too narrow to hold them. We find someone who writes and interprets in many volumes, yet not one of them has been able to reach the reality of what God intends. For if the Qur'an had come and poured out its gift in the century in which the Messenger lived, tell me, by God: how would later centuries receive it? It would be a reception devoid of care for it, because it would be repetitive speech.

So He has explained everything in it, and every person and every age takes from it according to the measure of its mind. And if the Qur'an were to be interpreted, no one would interpret it except the one upon whom it descended, our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Could anyone after that say anything in tafsir? So if the Messenger (ﷺ) had interpreted it fully, he would have frozen it, because no one would dare to bring an interpretation after the Messenger.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) knew that the gifts of the Qur'an are endless, so he did not interpret it fully. Rather, he clarified it with what contemporary minds could bear, so that they would not turn away from it. And if the Qur'an had said: "The earth is a sphere and it revolves around the sun," would anyone have believed it? Even now there are those who deny that. Instead we find the Qur'an alluding to it with a light allusion, until minds are broad enough for it. The Truth says:

﴿He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night.﴾ (part of 39:5)

Since the night comes after the day, and the day comes after the night, in the form of a near-sphere, the shape upon which night and day come is the shape of a sphere. It is as if each of night and day revolves after the other around a sphere. So the Truth gives the hint with a measure, so that minds may be broad enough to understand. The Qur'an says:

﴿To God belong the east and the west.﴾ (part of 2:142)

This is a clear statement, because each of us knows east and west. But when the Truth says:

﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests.﴾ (55:17) (Surah al-Rahman)

Would a contemporary of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) understand it? Yes, because when he says: "The sun rose from such-and-such a place and set over another place," then at its rising for you it sets for me, and when it sets for you it rises for me, and thus every east has with it a west. So the saying of God, "Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests," is true.

We know that the sun has a rising point every day. Whoever visits, in Upper Egypt, the temple that has 365 openings, windows, and sees that the sun rises each day from a particular opening and does not rise from the other openings, becomes certain that the sun has a different rising point each day. So there are easts and wests, and God, the Speaker, spoke truly: "Lord of the easts and the wests."

The Qur'an addresses us in a manner that the contemporary mind can bear, and when something new arises, we find the matter stored in the Qur'an; we find a new interpretation that does not abrogate the other interpretation but elevates it.

So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not wish to interpret the Qur'an in full, because he had to interpret it in what his contemporary minds could bear, and if he interpreted it in what his contemporary minds could bear, that would mean he would not give later minds nourishment from the Qur'an. Therefore the Messenger (ﷺ) left the Qur'an uninterpreted except for a small portion. You find this in the verses of the cosmos, while in the rulings the matter is defined.

But in the matters in which knowledge is renewed, he left them. Therefore the Prophet (peace be upon him) said about the Qur'an: "Its wonders do not cease" (la tanqadi 'ajaibuh), as if he is drawing our attention to the fact that its wonders do not end or finish, and every day it gives new wonders. So the Qur'an is blessed by virtue of what is stored in it until the Hour. And you turn to the people and find them toiling to discover the secrets of the cosmos, and you find that the Qur'an has touched what they seek with a light touch.

﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed, confirming what was before it.﴾ (part of 6:92)

When you say "between the hands of a thing" (bayna yadayi al-shay'), you mean the thing that precedes, and the earlier books are those that descended before the Qur'an, that is, before it. What is meant by them are the well-known, famous books, namely the Torah and the Gospel, since they are the two books that remain until now.

The Qur'an confirms what is before it, and this does not mean confirming the distorted (al-muharraf) but confirming the original (al-asil). For this reason we find Abdullah ibn Salam and others, when they came to Islam, acknowledged this. Abdullah ibn Salam said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "My breast has been opened to Islam, but I know that the Jews are a people of slander (bahtun), that is, they are obstinate. So I want you to ask them about me before I embrace Islam." The Messenger of Allah said to them: "What do you say about Abdullah ibn Salam?" They said: "Our rabbi, son of our rabbi, our elder, and our chief...," etc.

Then the man said: "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." Here they began pouring insults upon our master Abdullah ibn Salam, and he said: "Did I not tell you, O Messenger of Allah, that they are a people of slander?"

And the Truth's saying: ﴿confirming what was before it﴾ means that if you want to know the truth of this matter, then bring forth what they have no need to deny, and you will find the Qur'an has come in agreement with it. An example of this: when the Qur'an came with stoning (rajm). They tried to lighten the ruling of stoning, because a woman had committed adultery and they wished to show her favor. They referred her case to the Prophet, and some of them said to others: "If he rules against stoning, this is good for us and for her." And strangely, they do not believe in Muhammad, yet they want a ruling from him. The Messenger (peace be upon him) said to them: "Bring the Torah," and they brought the scrolls they had, and they found the verse of stoning. So the Qur'an confirms what is before it, without concealment, without distortion, and without misinterpretation.

And if you look at the issues to which they turn their attention, but which pass before them in a flash, you will find that these issues are a means by which God intends to expose corruption, lying and tyranny, so that the people of falsehood do not obliterate the landmarks of truth. Such issues require a skilled and perceptive investigator. And we find that He, glorified is He, mentioned in the Torah an example for the Muhammadan community, and repeats this example in the Qur'an when He, glorified is He, says:

﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him are severe against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves.﴾ (part of 48:29) (Surah al-Fath)

When we look at the words (ashidda', "severe") and (ruhama', "merciful"), we find on the surface an apparent contradiction in disposition. But the careful investigator knows from this statement that Islam does not shape the Muslim into one single color, because it wants from him all colors. If it had created him severe, he would lose the places of mercy, and if it had made him merciful, he would lose the places of firmness. Islam requires the Muslim to adhere to spiritual and material values so that each guards the other, because if Muslims went to matter alone, their civilization would become savagery, and if they went to values alone, they would not be able to establish a civilization that endures and lasts. The Truth wants a civilization that combines the two, the spirit and the matter. Therefore Islam combines the two, the spirit and the matter, because the Jews in their understanding of them lost the spirit, and the Christians in their understanding of them drowned in spirituality and lost the material. The Qur'an came confirming what was before it. Thus the verse came with the message concerning the People of the Book.

The message continues to the people of Quraysh, residents of Makkah, saying: ﴿so that you may warn the Mother of Cities﴾. We know that Umm al-Qura means Makkah. Some have tried to take this verse as proof that the Qur'an was sent down only to the community of the Arabs. To these we say: you have not understood well the implications of the wording. Let us ask: what is al-hawl (the surroundings) first? Al-hawl is the surrounding that encircles a point, any point and every point, and around every point there is a radius, which may be twenty kilometers, and may be a hundred kilometers, and whenever the area extends further, it is around this point. So the word al-hawl includes everything around it, and the surroundings of every place include every place.

And why was it called Umm al-Qura? Either because Hajar, when she settled

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 6, verse 93:

Then the Truth (al-Haqq) says:

﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah, or says, "I have been inspired," when nothing has been inspired to him, or who says, "I will reveal the like of what Allah has revealed"? If you could but see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death, and the angels extend their hands, [saying], "Discharge your souls! Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation for what you used to say about Allah other than the truth, and for being arrogant toward His signs." (93)﴾.

When the Truth (al-Haqq) comes in the form of a rhetorical question, the purpose is not to ask. He, glorified is He, does not want the information to come from Himself, though He is able to say: "The one who fabricates is a wrongdoer." But here He brings the question that affirms that there is no one more unjust than the one who fabricates a lie against Allah, and Allah presents the matter to the believers as if He were asking, so that every believer presents the matter to his mind and deduces the answer. If the one who fabricates a lie against his fellow and his equal is punished, then what of the one who fabricates against Allah? When you hear this speech: ﴿Who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah﴾, and you review the matter, you will not find anyone more unjust than him. In this way Allah draws out the judgment from the mouth of the one who is addressed.

And how does a person fabricate a lie against Allah? Such as when he conveys to people and claims and says: "I am a prophet," and he is not. Here is the ultimate fabrication against Allah. Beware of thinking that he is lying to people; no, he is lying against Allah, because he has asserted that Allah has sent him when Allah has not sent him.

Al-Iftira' (fabrication): a deliberate, intentional lie. This applies to the claimed prophethoods, such as Musaylima al-Kadhdhab, Sajah, Tulayha al-Asadi, and al-Aswad al-Ansi. All of these claimed prophethood, and yet no one asked them for a miracle indicating their prophethood, because each one of them, when he announced his prophethood, brought what would lighten the rulings of religion for the people.

One said: "I lighten the prayer, and zakat has no need." Therefore, everyone who wished to be relieved of the commands and prohibitions of religion followed them, convincing himself that he was religious, without committing himself to the obligations of religiousness. This is the reason why the adherents of false prophethoods and baseless claims find supporters among the hypocrites. One of these followers may be cultured, and then believes a deceiving prophet. If you asked the follower of the deceiver and said to him: "Did you ask this claimant to prophethood, 'What is your miracle?'" – and this is the first condition of prophethood – you would never find anyone who asked this question. Why?

Because religiosity is a natural disposition in the soul, but what makes religiosity difficult are the obligations that religiosity imposes. When the weak-souled follower sees that there is someone who relieves him of religious obligations, makes him understand that he is upon religion, and reduces the obligations upon him, weak-souled people follow him, and the matter becomes chaos.

﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah, or says, "I have been inspired," when nothing has been inspired to him﴾ (part of verse 93, Surat al-An'am).

There was one who claimed and said: "I am a prophet," and said: "I will reveal the like of this Qur'an." What did this claimant say – and he was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith – in a nation whose ear is rhetorical, affected by the music of words: "By those who grind with a grind, by those who knead with a kneading, by those who bake with a baking!" !! And why did he not begin the matter from its beginning and say: "By those who sow with a sowing, by those who plough with a ploughing"? Then he would say, the one who claimed to have been inspired: "By those who knead with a kneading, by those who bake with a baking," and he should have followed it also with: "By those who eat with an eating, by those who digest with a digesting."

Of course this speech was a kind of empty nonsense, because the Truth sends down its speech measured, attractive with meanings that have their worth in the information. Therefore the true word was revealed: ﴿or says, "I have been inspired," when nothing has been inspired to him﴾. And there came one, 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh al-Qurashi, who was a foster-brother of our master 'Uthman, and who was a scribe of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and sat in the presence of the Prophet. Then the verse was revealed:

﴿And We created man from an extract of clay. Then We placed him as a sperm-drop in a secure place. Then We made the sperm-drop into a clinging clot, then We made the clot into a lump of flesh, then We made the lump into bones, then We clothed the bones with flesh; then We produced him as another creation﴾ (Surat al-Mu'minun).

He was amazed at the stages in which the Truth created man, and said: ﴿So blessed be Allah, the best of creators﴾. The Messenger of Allah said to him: "Write it down, for it has been revealed." The man was deluded and said: "If Muhammad is truthful, then I have been inspired just as he was inspired; and if he is lying, then I have said as he said." So the Messenger of Allah ordered his blood to be forfeited, and said to his companions: "Whoever sees him, let him kill him." On the year of the conquest, 'Uthman radiya Allahu 'anhu brought him, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, pardon 'Abd Allah." The Messenger of Allah was silent. 'Uthman radiya Allahu 'anhu said: "Pardon him." The Messenger of Allah was silent. He repeated it a third time: "Pardon him, O Messenger of Allah." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Yes."

Our master 'Uthman had a special status with the Messenger of Allah, and the Messenger gestured toward our master 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, so the man took him and departed. When he had departed, the Messenger said to his companions: "Did I not tell you, whoever sees him, let him say so?" Our master 'Abbad ibn Bishr said: "O Messenger of Allah, I had turned my sight to you – that is, I directed my eyes to you – so that you would indicate to me to kill him." The Messenger of Allah said to 'Abbad ibn Bishr: (It is not fitting for a prophet that he have the treachery of the eyes.) Ibn Abi Sarh became Muslim and his Islam was good.

And who says "I will reveal the like of what Allah has revealed," and what are the punishments of those who fabricate lies against Allah and attempt to deceive people, claiming that Allah has sent them inspiration?

The Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿If you could but see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death, and the angels extend their hands, [saying], "Discharge your souls! Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation for what you used to say about Allah other than the truth, and for being arrogant toward His signs."﴾ (part of verse 93, Surat al-An'am).

When you hear this "if" (law), know that it is conditional, and you say, for example: "If so-and-so comes to me, I would honour him." When we read the Qur'an we find that many instances of "law" have no apodosis (answer). Why? Because stating the answer confines the answer within a spoken scope; but if you intend an answer that words cannot confine, you leave it to the listener, just as you find a young man playing the role of the local bully in the neighbourhood and troubling its residents, then he falls into the hands of the police who take him to punish him, and one of those who had seen him before, who had been troubled by him, says: "Ah, if you had seen the bully boy in the hands of the police!"

Where is the answer of the condition here? It does not come, because it encompasses a marvellous matter that the style is too narrow to express.

The Truth, glorified and exalted is He, says here: ﴿If you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death﴾. He did not say: "What would you see?" Because you would see a wonder that speech cannot convey. And "al-ghamarat" (agonies) are the severity from which a person cannot find release or escape.

The Truth continues: ﴿and the angels extend their hands, [saying], "Discharge your souls!"﴾. Are these the angels of death who seize the soul, or is the speech about the angels of punishment? It includes both kinds: the angels who seize the soul and the angels of punishment.

﴿and the angels extend their hands, [saying], "Discharge your souls!"﴾ It is as if the angels of seizing the soul say to them: If you were stubborn toward Allah in many rulings, you were stubborn toward Allah in faith, you were stubborn toward Allah in affirming the Messenger; here Allah has commanded us to seize your souls. Are you able to rebel against the decrees of the Truth? If you are, let each of you display his skill in resisting the seizing of his soul; or the angels exaggerate in afflicting them, as if we were to say to someone: "Strangle yourself and draw your soul out with your own hand," or: "Get your souls out of the punishment that encircles you."

"Adhab al-Hawn" (the punishment of humiliation) is the painful punishment that contains abasement. The modes of punishment in the Qur'an are varied: it says once "the punishment of humiliation" (al-adhab al-muhin), or "and He has prepared for them a humiliating punishment" (adhaban muhinan), or "for them a painful punishment" (adhab alim). So sometimes the punishment is painful but without abasement, and sometimes it is painful and contains abasement. Just as blessing contains honour, so retribution contains abasement. Let me give this example – and to Allah belongs the highest example, for Allah is exalted above any likeness: we may find a ruler who imprisons a person and orders that the detainee be placed in a palace with a lavish garden, but when the food comes, the guard says to him: "Take, poison," and in that there is great humiliation.

Why does the Truth make them taste the humiliating punishment? The answer comes from Allah: ﴿for what you used to say about Allah other than the truth, and for being arrogant toward His signs.﴾ As when one says: "I have been inspired," when nothing has been inspired to him. And they also act arrogantly toward the signs that natural reason believes in. The Truth says:

﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and arrogance﴾ (part of verse 14, Surat al-Naml).

The Exalted says next:

﴿And you have come to Us alone, as We created you the first time, and you have left behind what We bestowed upon you, behind your backs. And We do not see with you your intercessors whom you claimed to be partners [in your affairs]. Certainly your relations have been severed among you, and lost from you is what you used to claim.﴾ (6:94)

His saying, the Truth: ﴿And you have come to Us alone﴾ means that each one of you comes to God alone, separated from what he had in his worldly life of wealth, children or followers. Each of them came to God without the idols which he claimed were partners with God and which he took as his intercessors. ("Furada," "fardan," and "farid") — "furada" is the plural of "fardan" or "farid," like "sukara" is the plural of "sakran" and "asara" is the plural of "asir." They come to God in groups and multitudes, but each of them came alone, separated from what he had in the world of wealth, family, children and followers, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿and you have left behind what We bestowed upon you, behind your backs.﴾

"Khawwala" means He made for him servants from among followers and disciples, and [it applies to] those who were restricted in provision and those who lived in His blessing. Each of them came alone, separated from what he had in the world, just as God created you the first time, that is, just as you entered the world!

﴿And you have come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾ (part of 6:94).

His saying, the Truth: ﴿You have come to Us﴾ means that the person who sinned almost presents himself to punishment, confessing that he deserves this punishment, acknowledging his sin. It is as if a person is overcome by grief over what he did and by rebuke of his own self, which turned away from the truth, so he says to himself: "You deserve the punishment."

﴿And you have left behind what We bestowed upon you, behind your backs. And We do not see with you your intercessors whom you claimed to be partners [in your affairs]. Certainly your relations have been severed among you﴾ (part of 6:94).

"Al-bayn" is that which separates or that which connects. When we find two people sitting with "bayn" between them, this "bayn" is both separating and connecting. If you consider it connecting, I say: "This has been severed," meaning the severing has occurred between you two, and the bonds among you have been broken and your unity scattered. If "bayn" is separating, then they connected themselves with the idols.

And what was the relationship of these people with the idols they associated in worship? They used to offer sacrifices to them, and other things. These idols, and everyone they made a partner with God, will disown them on the Day of Resurrection. Thus His saying, the Truth, is fulfilled: ﴿Certainly your relations have been severed among you.﴾

He, glorified be He, continues: ﴿And lost from you is what you used to claim.﴾ "Dalla" means went astray and disappeared; what you used to be concerned with, so you do not find them, as evidenced by His saying, the Truth:

﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed﴾ (part of 2:166).

Allah says: ﴿Verily, Allah is the splitter of the grain and the date-stone. He brings forth the living from the dead, and brings forth the dead from the living. That is Allah; so how are you deluded away?﴾ (95)

After the Truth has spoken about tawhid (the oneness of God) and prophethood, and about those who opposed, contradicted and rejected these prophecies and spoke falsehood concerning them, Allah wished to draw His creatures' attention to what He has prepared for them to sustain their lives, and how He has subjected to them the whole of the cosmos with all that is in it: inanimate matter, plants and animals. It is as if He, glory be to Him, is clarifying: if you do not see that the Creator deserves to be worshipped, then look at the blessings He has bestowed upon you. Since the created servant has all the blessings of the Supreme Creator, why does he not hear His word, glory be to Him? O creature, you are being nourished at the table of the Most Merciful, and He is your Creator. So look, reflect and recognise.

﴿Verily, Allah is the splitter of the grain and the date-stone.﴾ When you hear the word of majesty (lafz al-jalala), namely "Allah", it is the name of the Necessarily Existent Being. You must take the word "Allah" with all that it indicates of the attributes of majesty and the attributes of beauty, whether you know them or not, because He, glory be to Him, created the whole cosmos and is its Sustainer (al-Qayyum). This creation and this sustaining is an act that requires multiple attributes: power, wisdom, vast knowledge, mercy, expansion and restriction, and other things. Instead of bringing you the attributes of power and beauty and enumerating them, He, glory be to Him, names Himself "Allah", because it is the all-comprehensive name for all His attributes. In the beginning of every action we say: "In the name of Allah" (bismillah), and in this there is a concise statement of what any action requires. Any action requires power, so you say: "In the name of the Powerful (al-Qadir)." It requires knowledge, so you say: "In the name of the All-Knowing (al-'Alim)." It requires wisdom, so you say: "In the name of the All-Wise (al-Hakim)." It requires might, so you say: "In the name of the Mighty (al-'Aziz)." It may require subduing your enemy, because you may enter into war with him, so you say: "In the name of the Subduer (al-Qahir)." Thus every action requires a host of attributes of perfection and majesty to serve the deed. Instead of saying "in the name of the Powerful, in the name of the All-Knowing, in the name of the Restrainer", He, glory be to Him, spares you all of that, so you say: "In the name of Allah", because the name of majesty, "Allah", is the one that comprises all the attributes of perfection.

﴿Verily, Allah is the splitter of the grain and the date-stone.﴾ "Faliq" means "splitter" (shaqq), making each of the grain and the stone into two halves (fiqlatain). "Habb" (grain) refers to that which has no stone, such as barley, wheat and rice. There is also that which has a stone, such as dates and peaches, and within the heart of the stone you find something else. There is another kind which has seeds, such as watermelon, and within a seed you find something too. Thus the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, clarifies to you: My greatness is manifested in that I create the grain and I create the stone. There are also ready-split grains, such as the fava bean and the lentil.

When you look at this process, you find something wondrous!

When you take a date-stone or a barley grain and place it in the earth, in its appropriate environment, with a little moisture, you find that from its two halves there has emerged a plant, and the stone almost splits, so that the weak shoot (al-zaban) emerges from between the two halves and forms what is called the radicle (al-judhayr). Thus you find the secret of life comes from the two halves; if you remove this radicle, life ends. For this reason, we find people wondering when they break into ant nests and find small white crumbs of fragmented grain beside the nest, and they discover that these are the shoots of the grain that the ants bring into the nest. For if the ants brought in the whole grains, a drop of moisture might come and this grain would grow, becoming a tree that destroys the nest. So who guided the ant to act in this way? It is Allah. And we find the ant splitting a coriander (al-kuzbara) seed into four pieces, because if it split it into two, it might germinate. Who taught it? It is He, glory be to Him:

﴿Who created and proportioned, and who determined and guided﴾ (Surat al-A'la, 2–3).

And what is remarkable is that when you see the weak shoot at the moment it emerges into life, which will afterwards become a root, it is fragile and weak; if you hold it in your hand you crush it, yet it pierces the heart of the hard earth which, if you struck it with a knife, would break the knife. But the weak radicle enters into the heart of rock and earth. So what power gave it that? What power pierces the earth for it? Is it the radicle that pierced the earth, or was it pierced for it? The Truth has split the earth for the seed, so that from it it may extract nourishment for the crop. It is the power of the Truth, glory be to Him: ﴿the splitter of the grain﴾, which has stored in two halves sustenance for the plant, which, when moisture touches it, the young shoot feeds upon until the roots grow, and the plant draws its nourishment from the two halves until it becomes firm and established in the earth, after which the two halves turn into two green leaves.

The Truth, glory be to Him, continues: ﴿He brings forth the living from the dead, and brings forth the dead from the living.﴾ When the scholars contemplated this statement and wished to clarify for us what the living is and what the dead is, they all failed to define what life is. Life is the subsistence of an existent thing in carrying out its task. Human life includes movement, sensation and running; then there is a second life in animals, a third life in plants, and a life of a different character in inanimate matter. As we were taught in schools, when the teacher held a magnetized rod to attract iron filings, even hard iron has a certain form of life. We have all seen in school the glass tube into which they put iron filings, and how they are affected by the magnet rod, becoming aligned and arranged in one level. Thus we know that life is the energy present in every being so that it may carry out its task. Even stones differ in forms of life: there is a stone that takes the form of marble, and another that takes the form of alabaster, and every kind of stone has a form of life.

We read in the Qur'an:

﴿That whoever perishes may perish upon clear proof, and whoever lives may live upon clear proof﴾ (part of verse 42, Surat al-Anfal).

The Truth has set against perishing (al-halak) its opposite, which is life; perishing is the opposite of life and life is the opposite of perishing. He, glory be to Him, says in another verse:

﴿Everything perishes except His Face﴾ (part of verse 88, Surat al-Qasas).

Therefore, since everything is perishing, everything has life. The error is to think that every life resembles human life in sensation and movement; no, life in everything is according to its nature, until the Resurrection. Every living thing has a life suited to it. When we hear:

﴿There is not a thing but that it exalts His praise, but you do not understand their glorification﴾ (part of verse 44, Surat al-Isra'),

we say: yes, everything that glorifies His praise says something. Beware of saying that this glorification is merely an indication (dalalah) of the Creator, for some say: "This is glorification as an indication of the Creator." We say: if what Allah intended were glorification as a mere indication of a Creator, He would not have said: ﴿but you do not understand their glorification﴾.

So none of us understands the language of glorification. We have known from before, when Solomon, peace be upon him, heard the speech of the ant and smiled laughing at it; likewise what he heard from the hoopoe, and likewise the subjection of the mountains to glorify with David, peace be upon him.

﴿Verily, Allah is the splitter of the grain and the date-stone; He brings forth the living from the dead, and brings forth the dead from the living. That is Allah; so how are you deluded away?﴾ (95, Surat al-An'am)

Every word has its significance and meaning. The word "knowledge" indicates the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of everything in existence; the word "wisdom" indicates that everything issues from wisdom; the word "the Provider" (al-Razzaq) indicates that everything provided for in existence has taken from His overflow and goodness, and so on, without end, for the perfection of His essential attributes. The word "Allah" indicates all the attributes of majesty, beauty and perfection, so that when He says "Allah", this name comprises the Powerful, the Knowing, the Wise, the Capable, and all the attributes of the Truth, whether known to us or unknown, since His essence, glory be to Him and exalted, is characterized by all the attributes of perfection; it is necessary that every act issuing from His perfect essence possesses absolute power, beauty and perfection.

So when the Truth says this, He is drawing our attention to the fact that everything existing in being is from the creation of Allah, and that it has a life suited to its task. Man has a life suited to his task; the animal has a life suited to its task; the plant has a life suited to its task; inanimate matter has a life suited to its task. When you look at all things in this sense, you find that every existing thing has life, but the complete life with all its constituents is found in the highest of creatures, which is man. Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, created in man life in terms of sensation and movement, then gave him another life which rises above mere life and gives his life value. For the life we live is enjoyed by both believer and disbeliever, and at most it gives sensation and movement for the span of our lives in this world. But the life of faith, by what Allah sends us of a method through the hand of the Messenger, gives us a wider, more enduring and more abundant life, and this is the true life. For this reason the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And indeed the Last Abode is the Life, if only they knew﴾ (part of verse 64, Surat al-'Ankabut).

This is the real life. The word of the Truth, ﴿Verily, Allah is the splitter of the grain and the date-stone﴾, is the first premise for life; then He speaks of life, that He brings forth the living from the dead. Here He has addressed us according to the measure of our primary knowledge of things: a thing that has no sensation or movement we consider dead; but if you look at the reality, you will find that everything in existence has life. The confirmation of this is His saying, majestic is His power: ﴿Everything perishes except His Face﴾.

And since everything is perishing, everything before it perishes had life in it.

Allah, glory be to Him, says:

﴿Say: O Allah, Owner of the Kingdom, You give the kingdom to whom You will and You take the kingdom from whom You will; You exalt whom You will and You abase whom You will; in Your hand is the good; indeed You are Powerful over all things. You cause the night to enter the day and You cause the day to enter the night; You bring forth the living from the dead and You bring forth the dead from the living; and You provide for whom You will without account﴾ (Al 'Imran, 26–27).

Why, in this verse, did He use "takhruj" (bringing forth), and in the verse we are contemplating He used "wa-mukhriju al-mayyit min al-hayy" (and brings forth the dead from the living)? Those who have researched this have looked superficially at the partial correspondence in the verse: "He brings forth the living from the dead" and then "and brings forth the dead from the living", and forgotten that He, glory be to Him, said that He brings forth the living from the dead in order to show that Allah splits the grain and the date-stone so that He may bring forth the living from the dead; that is, Allah split and cleaved the grain and the stone in order that the living might be brought forth from the dead.

Then He said: ﴿and brings forth the dead from the living﴾, which is the counterpart of "splitter", so do not take it as a partial correspondence within the verse. And because the name indicates permanence, while the verb indicates occurrence: the Truth, glory be to Him, has an attribute in His essence and an attribute in the objects related to that essence. He, glory be to Him, is the Provider (raziq) before there is any creature to be provided for; He is the Provider, and after He has created those who are provided for, He is still the Provider, because He is the Creator, and "Creator" is an attribute of the essence even if the object of the attribute does not yet exist. He is the Giver of life (al-Muhyi) before there is anyone whom He gives life, because His attribute in His essence is to give life; and the Causer of death (al-Mumit) before He causes to die anyone He wills to cause to die, because the attribute exists in His essence.

Glory be to Him, the Splitter of the grain and the date-stone: that is, before the grain and the stone that He splits exist. And the bringing forth of the living from the dead is a fixed attribute in His essence before its object exists. He also has an attribute after its object exists. So if He intends the attribute before the object exists, He uses the names: "Splitter" (faliq) and "Bringer forth" (mukhrij). And if He intends the attribute after it exists, He says: "yukhriju" (He brings forth), "yukhriju" (He brings forth).

The Truth concludes the verse: ﴿That is Allah; so how are you deluded away?﴾ (95, Surat al-An'am).

"Dha" (that) is a demonstrative pronoun referring to what has preceded: He, glory be to Him, is the Splitter of the grain and the date-stone, and the One who brings forth the living from the dead and the dead from the living, and He is Allah. The kaf in His saying "dhalikum" is for those addressed, namely us; the lam in "dhalikum" is for distance, and the mim is for the plural. When the Truth wishes to address His Messenger, He says:

﴿That is the Book, there is no doubt in it﴾ (part of verse 2, Surat al-Baqarah).

But He addresses us, saying "dhalikum", as an indication of the words of the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted: Allah, and the Splitter, and the Bringer forth, and the address is to the bulk of those addressed by the Qur'an. So if Allah has these attributes, how do they turn away from believing in Him and affirming His oneness? He has mentioned to us the first constituent of life, which is plants, which is what we eat.
