And they persisted in disbelief by mentioning the names of the idols over them: ﴿and cattle over which they do not mention the name of Allah, fabricating against Him..﴾ (6:138)

This is a kind of fabrication they committed, attributing it to something received from Allah and commanded by Him, glorified is He. Had they said that these matters were of their own making, the gravity of the fabrication would have been lessened. But it is a severe fabrication, because they brought these things and attributed them to Allah, and they had departed from the religion and said that some of their conduct was from the religion. Therefore Allah will recompense them for what they fabricated, confirming His saying:

﴿..He will recompense them for what they used to fabricate.﴾ (6:138)

Almighty Allah then says:

﴿They say, "What is in the wombs of these livestock is exclusively for our males, and forbidden to our wives; but if it is stillborn, then they all share in it. He will surely recompense them for their description. Indeed, He is All-Wise, All-Knowing."﴾

Falsehood leads them to another falsehood. They claimed that what is in the wombs of these livestock, namely the milk and the fetuses, if born alive, belongs only to their males, and the women may not eat any of it at all. But if any of it was stillborn, both men and women ate it. This indicates arbitrariness in the division.

Almighty Allah concludes the verse with the noble statement:

﴿... He will surely recompense them for their description. Indeed, He is All-Wise, All-Knowing.﴾ [Surah al-An'am]

That is, He will recompense them for their lying and fabrication with a fitting punishment for liars, because He, glorified is He, is (Wise) in His actions, His words and His decree, and (All-Knowing) of what they do of good and evil. He will reward them for what they have done with the most complete and perfect recompense.

The True One (Allah) says after that:

﴿Those who have lost are those who killed their children foolishly, without knowledge, and forbade what Allah had provided for them, fabricating against Allah. They have certainly gone astray, and they were not guided.﴾ (140)

The nature of the loss is that they did not consider that Allah provides for them and for their children as well. Perhaps you, O father, have killed a child who, had he lived, would have lived by His provision in abundance. Often some children are a source of abundant provision, and of such a son it is said that his face is the face of good fortune, prosperity and blessing. From the day he is born, he is born with good in him. This is so that a person does not turn away from the giving of Allah, because when you turn away from the giving of Allah, you deprive yourself of a giving in what you think is not a giving, and this is a great loss.

We observe that the Arabs lived in an environment that responded to the cry for help. When someone in distress cries out and seeks aid, he finds someone to rescue him, and the most entitled to come to his rescue are a man's family and children. An example of this is what happened to the Messenger's grandfather (ﷺ) when he went to dig the well. The Quraysh came and stood in his way so that he would not dig it, and he said: "If I had ten sons, I would sacrifice one of them." Thus, the abundance of children in such matters gives strength and multiplies those who answer the cry for help, and only one who is innately disposed to rescue does this.

If you kill a child out of fear of poverty, you may lose a provision that may lie within the offspring you kill, and besides that, you lose the splendour of status, the strength, or the family. Or at least they have lost, because they opposed the purposes of Allah in creation through procreation.

﴿Those who have lost are those who killed their children foolishly, without knowledge..﴾ (140)

"Safahan" (سفها) means recklessness, folly, and ignorance.

﴿..and forbade what Allah had provided for them, fabricating against Allah. They have certainly gone astray, and they were not guided.﴾ (140) [Surat al-An'am]

When they forbid for themselves what Allah has provided them of livestock, they are people of folly and error and loss. If they had left them alone, they would have benefited from them in carrying their loads, or in the milk they yield, or in eating their meat. In their folly and ignorance, they have lost much, and besides that, they did what they did through deliberate lying against Allah. They have gone astray (ضلوا أةنمنتااتا)

They were not fit for guidance. It would have sufficed to describe them with His saying "they have gone astray," but He added "and they were not guided," because error is not reaching the destination that leads to the goal, and this may happen through ignorance of the path. But the True One, glory be to Him, had laid out for them the path of truth, yet they preferred to go towards error despite the existence of the path of truth.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 6, verse 141:

Then He, glory be to Him, says:

﴿It is He who produces gardens, both trellised and untrellised, and the palm trees and crops of varying produce, and the olives and pomegranates, similar and dissimilar. Eat of their fruit when they bear fruit, and pay its due on the day of its harvest, and do not be excessive. Indeed, He does not like the excessive.﴾ (141)

The word of the Truth: "Anshaʼa" (produced) means He brought into existence with an originality that has no precedent. There were no models that God, glory be to Him, followed; rather He initiated them without any prior example, because there is no creator other than Him. The Creator, when there is no one besides Him, no partner or equal, when He creates, He creates a creation not according to a system or pattern that preceded Him.

The word "jannāt" (gardens) points to the specific place we know, which gathers the various kinds of crops and fruits that we subsist on and that we enjoy. It is called a janna and called jannāt, because the whole root indicates concealment and covering. From it comes "junūn" (madness), because it contains a concealment of the intellect; and from it "al-jinn," because they are hidden from the sight of the eye; and likewise "al-mijann" (shield), because it conceals from a person the stabs of the opponent.

The janna is the place filled with crops and fruits, in which the trees rise high, and their branches and boughs thicken and intertwine so that they conceal whoever is inside and also conceal him from the rest of the places, because he has no need of other places. In the janna are all the necessities of life: food, fruit, pasture, water, greenery and enjoyment; and in it is everything. It is also called "qaṣr" (palace), the great, complete house that encompasses and includes all the facilities, because it confines you (qaṣaraka) from any other place, since in it are all the things you need, so you need nothing beyond it.

﴿It is He who produces gardens, both trellised..﴾ (141) [Surat al-An'am]

The root ʻ-r-sh (ʻarsh) indicates height, and from it the ceiling is called "ʻarsh." The word ʻarsh is also used for a couch, as in His word: ﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne﴾; and it is used for sovereignty, as in His word: ﴿And she has a great throne﴾. All of this indicates "height." His word here: ﴿trellised and untrellised﴾ means that the vine is a kind of crop which, when we mean to cultivate it, we provide the poles and supports on which it stands, because the extension of its soft branches cannot stand up by itself. But there is also another kind that stands by itself, which we call the wild grape, and it seems the discussion concerns the vineyard. That is: if you look at the crops that have no stalk, such as watermelon, cantaloupe and squash, and all crops that have no stalk, you will find them spread on the ground, that is, not standing on bases, poles or trellises. Although we now try to raise them to give them productive strength. The speech came in accordance with what existed among the Arabs at the time of the Prophet's mission (ﷺ): ﴿It is He who produces gardens, both trellised and untrellised, and the palm trees and crops﴾. The word "zarʻ" (crops) is used to mean what we subsist on of grains.

﴿of varying produce, and the olives and pomegranates, similar and dissimilar..﴾ (141) [Surat al-An'am].

When we look at this verse, we find that it was preceded by a verse containing all these meanings. He, glory be to Him, says:

﴿It is He who sends down water from the sky, and We bring forth by it the growth of every thing; then We bring forth from it green foliage, from which We bring forth grain piled up; and from the palm tree, from its spathe, clusters hanging low; and gardens of grapes, and the olive and the pomegranate, similar and dissimilar. Look at its fruit when it bears fruit and its ripening. Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾ (99) [Surat al-An'am].

Some people try to criticize the Qur'an, saying that it repeats the same meanings, because they do not possess the insight that the speaker is God, who speaks about everything for a wise purpose. Here He speaks about these things as evidence of the Creator and His oneness, as proven by His concluding the verse with His word: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾ But the speech in the verse that we are now reflecting upon has come with the intent of speaking about benefiting from them, so He says: ﴿Eat of its fruit when it bears fruit and pay its due on the day of its harvest﴾ (part of verse 141, Surat al-An'am).

There is no doubt that the soundness of belief in the One God requires evidence first, because its benefit is more comprehensive, more general, deeper, and more enduring than eating, since eating at most sustains us in this life, whereas the first proofs give us lasting reward and enduring bliss. Therefore the first verse is related to evidence, and this verse is related to benefit. Here we note that He said: ﴿Eat of its fruit when it bears fruit﴾, and in this is permission to partake of things from it before they ripen, without this entailing any kind of harm; otherwise we would treat it with what removes and negates harm from us. So if you find fruits that have not ripened, it is permitted for you to eat from them. The Truth has not placed upon us any hardship regarding what we plough, sow and irrigate; rather God, glory be to Him, is the One who causes it to grow and we eat from it. The people of the countryside roast corn before it ripens, and He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿and pay its due on the day of its harvest.﴾

They have said that the verse is specific to what is reaped, which is crops, whereas things of which one does not say "harvested," such as fruits, are excluded from that. But Imam Abu Hanifa rejects this and holds that everything the earth produces falls under this text, because it is not correct to take the meaning of harvest according to custom, but according to the understanding of the language.

What is the meaning of "ḥaṣād" (harvest) linguistically? Ḥaṣād in language means cutting. So when you separate the desired fruit, this is harvesting. But the day of harvesting grains is when the produce is in the ears (of grain); and Imam Abu Hanifa holds that one should give from the very beginning to those present at the division, and likewise when you thresh and winnow it you give, and when you sift the grains you also give. The harvest begins from the moment you measure, and what precedes it is not counted. What you give of the right on the day of its harvest is other than what is obligatory; because He did not say "the known right," and in this there is an expansion of the scope of the extension of good to non-farmers.

﴿and do not be excessive. Indeed, He does not like the excessive.﴾ (part of verse 141, Surat al-An'am). Excess (isrāf) is transgressing the limit. Some have interpreted isrāf as mere increase, but the reality is that any transgression of the limit, whether by increase or decrease, is called isrāf, because it is derived from "sarf al-māʼ" (the wasting of water), which is when water is released and goes to waste without benefit. Sayyiduna Mujahid says: If a person had a mountain like Abu Qubays made of gold, then spent it on what is permissible, it would be counted as excess; and if he spent a single dirham in disobedience to God, it would be counted as excess.

Thus the meaning of "and do not be excessive" is two things: do not exceed the limits the Truth has prescribed, by using this in disobedience; or do not be excessive in giving to the poor less than he deserves.

Hatim al-Ta'i was extremely generous, and people sat blaming him for this generosity. One of them said to him: "There is no good in excess." He replied to him: "Nor is there excess in good." That is, as long as it is in good, it is not excess.

If we take the matter according to both meanings, deficiency and excess, what prevents us from giving the poor more? The report tells that some people are seized by generosity and vigor for giving when they see the abundance of their produce and what God has bestowed upon them from the yield of their land. They give much, as Thabit ibn Qays did: he had fifty palm trees, harvested them all and gave them all to the poor, leaving nothing for his children. When the matter was raised to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he said to him: "Give, but do not be excessive." Why? Lest you later need what you gave and then regret that you gave it.

Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 6, verse 142:

Allah then says:

﴿And of the cattle are some for carrying and some for bedding. Eat of what Allah has provided for you, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾

After Allah spoke of His blessings upon us in agriculture and His blessings upon us in livestock, He said, "And of the cattle" — namely camels, cows and sheep — "are some for carrying" (ḥamūlah). The ḥamūlah is that which carries; it is said, "So-and-so is ḥamūl," meaning he bears a great deal. Allah says: ﴿And they carry your loads to a land you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves.﴾ [Surah an-Nahl, 16:7].

That which is carried upon its back is called ḥumūlah. Hence we say of a vehicle that transports, "its load is so-and-so tons." ﴿And of the cattle are some for carrying and some for bedding.﴾

We ride camels, load upon them the saddles and all our needs. "Farshan" (for bedding) means: the counterpart of the ḥamūlah. The ḥamūlah is that which is strong and able to bear loads. Whatever cannot bear a load, because it is too young or because it is no longer fit for that, when you look at it superficially you find it as though it were spread upon the ground. Or, "And of the cattle are some for carrying" — these are the ones that carry your goods to a land you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves. "And for bedding": that is, and of what you take for bedding, by weaving from their wool, fleece and hair what you spread out.

﴿And of the cattle are some for carrying and some for bedding. Eat of what Allah has provided for you, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾ [Surah al-An'am, 6:142].

In speaking of the cattle, He mentions carrying and bedding, and He also mentions the matter of eating, because we eat their meat, their milk and all dairy products. Thus the benefits are multiplied: they carry us, and we take from their wool, their fur and their hair the bedding. The wabar is the hair of camels, and the ṣūf is the wool of sheep; goat hair is distinguished by its sheen and by the separation between its strands.

We notice that He, glory be to Him, said in the first verse, "Eat," and in the second, "Eat," because that came after speaking of what they had forbidden to themselves from the provisions of Allah on earth. It was necessary to affirm this meaning and clarify it: the One who created is Allah, and the One who imposed obligations is Allah, so do not take permission for anything or prohibition of anything except from the One who created and the One who imposed obligations.

﴿Eat of what Allah has provided for you, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾ Satan is the one who whispers to them to oppose the method of Allah, and Satan's enmity is evident. Since the enmity is established from before, for he brought Adam and Eve down from the rank of obedience to the rank of disobedience and emboldened them to oppose, so that they left the Garden, it is obligatory that we be cautious in accepting this whispering.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 6, verse 143:

Then the Truth (al-Haqq) explains to us the livestock that we take as beasts of burden, or from which we take what is spread out (for carpets and such), so He said:

﴿Eight pairs: of the sheep two, and of the goats two. Say: "Has He forbidden the two males or the two females, or that which the wombs of the two females contain? Inform me with knowledge, if you are truthful."﴾

The word "azwaj" (أزواج), the plural of "zawj," and "zawj" is applied to a thing together with what is paired with it, such as "zawj al-na'l" (a pair of sandals). In our customs we take it to mean two, but in origin it is applied to one together with what is paired with it, except that there is no distinction between the two such that the benefit of one is not obtained without the other, yet neither is distinguished from the other, like a pair of socks, for example. In such a case, the language permits us to call the two "a pair" (zawj). But if there is a difference between the two, we do not say of the two: "zawj."

As for male and female among humans, it is true that they are joined in that each of them is a human being, but the male has a task and the female has a different task. As for socks, each "single" one of them we put on any foot, because there is no distinction between them. So the word "zawj" is applied, meaning one thing together with what is paired with it. And the Truth says: ﴿Dwell, you and your spouse, in the Garden...﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah]: the word "zawj" here is applied to Hawwa' (Eve); Adam is a "zawj" and Hawwa' is a "zawj." And the Truth is the one who says: ﴿And that He created the two spouses, the male and the female﴾ [Surah al-Najm].

He did not say of the two that they are "zawj," for otherwise He would have said: "He created the zawj, the male and the female." So the word "zawj" is applied to one together with what is paired with it, just as the word "tawam" (twin) is not said of two, but said of one with another; but for the two one says: "tawamani" (twins).

﴿Eight pairs: of the sheep two, and of the goats two...﴾ [Surah al-An'am].

"Of the sheep two" means its male and female: the male is called "kabsh" (ram) and the female "na'jah" (ewe). "Of the goats two": the male we call "tays" (billy goat), and the female we call "anzah" (she-goat). Thus we have four, and from here we understand that "zawj" signifies one and what is paired with it.

﴿...Say: "Has He forbidden the two males or the two females, or that which the wombs of the two females contain? Inform me with knowledge, if you are truthful."﴾ [Surah al-An'am]: Since you are the ones who forbid and permit, and you say that this is from God, then tell us: has He forbidden the two males or the two females? And he cannot give an answer, because He, glory be to Him, has forbidden neither this nor that. Therefore the matter was presented in the form of a question, and when a matter is presented in the form of a question, its meaning is that it is established, such that if you ask your opponent he will say nothing but what you expect; this is called the assertive question (al-istifham al-taqriri). The Truth says: ﴿Inform me with knowledge, if you are truthful﴾, meaning: tell me with knowledge of that prohibition, if you are people of truth, because you are not fit to prohibit; it is only He who creates and legislates who forbids and permits. So if you have knowledge, tell us this knowledge.

And of camels two and of cattle two. Say: "Has He forbidden the two males or the two females, or what the wombs of the two females contain? Or were you witnesses when Allah enjoined this upon you? Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah to mislead people without knowledge? Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people."

Then the Truth comes with the report on the remaining four of the livestock animals (al-an'am), so He says: "And of camels two and of cattle two." Among the cattle there is also a male and a female. The male of cattle we call thawrat (bulls), and some people err in calling the female "baqara" (cow). Indeed, baqara is a name for each of the two, the male and the female, and the ta' in baqara indicates a single unit, while the name of the female is thawra.

"And of camels two and of cattle two. Say: 'Has He forbidden the two males or the two females?'" You say: "We have not followed a messenger, and we were in a period without messengers, and no messenger came to us. Therefore there is no prohibition except from Allah, and the prohibition of Allah does not reach you except through a messenger." Rather, were you witnesses to the matter of the prohibition, meaning, did you see your Lord and behold Him when He commanded you with this prohibition, or are you the prophets? You deliberately lie against Allah in order to mislead people. Therefore, the Truth does not guide one who wrongs himself and wrongs people.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 6, verse 145:

He, glorified is He, says after that:

﴿Say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it, unless it be carrion, or blood poured forth, or the flesh of swine—for indeed it is impure—or an abomination, or that over which the name of other than Allah has been invoked. But whoever is compelled [by necessity], neither desiring nor transgressing, then indeed your Lord is Forgiving and Merciful."﴾ (6:145)

The Almighty has spoken of prohibition in many verses. There is the verse in which He said: ﴿Prohibited to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, that which has been dedicated to other than Allah, the strangled animal, the animal beaten to death, the animal that falls to its death, the animal gored to death, that which has been eaten by a predator except what you [have time to] slaughter, and what is sacrificed on stone altars...﴾ (5:3) [Surah al-Ma'idah].

And here, in the verse about which we are reflecting, we find the restriction to only four [categories], so He, glorified is He, says:

﴿Say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it, unless it be carrion, or blood poured forth, or the flesh of swine—for indeed it is impure—or an abomination, or that over which the name of other than Allah has been invoked..."﴾ (6:145) [Surah al-An'am].

So how does this text agree with the other text?!

To the one who says this we say: you do not distinguish between brevity (ijaz) and elaboration (itnab), nor between generalization (ijmal) and detail (tafsil). What is omitted in this verse is included within "carrion" (al-maytah), because the strangled animal, the animal that falls to its death, the animal gored to death, and what a predator has eaten are included, and what is sacrificed on stone altars and what is dedicated to other than Allah are present and included in the word "carrion."

Then: who says that the Qur'an is the sole source of legislation? Legislation also belongs to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), by delegation from Allah in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it...﴾ (59:7) [Surah al-Hashr].

So do not say that the prohibitions are limited only to this verse, for there are many prohibitions in it, as evidenced by the fact that Allah at times generalizes, so He prohibits for us the khaba'ith (filthy things); every khabith is therefore forbidden. We have said before that blood poured forth is forbidden, and blood poured forth is the flowing liquid that gushes, runs and spills at the moment of slaughter. Is there blood that is not poured forth? Yes: it is the blood which, in the strength of its coagulation, becomes an organ of the body, such as the liver and the spleen. For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Two carrions and two bloods have been made lawful to us: as for the two carrions, fish and locusts; and as for the two bloods, the liver and the spleen." (1) In another narration: fish and locusts.

By the logic of prohibiting carrion and blood, we would have to avoid eating fish that has died, and the liver and spleen. But Allah has made fish, locusts, the liver and the spleen lawful for us, because they do not harm the body. Fish and locusts have no flowing blood (nafs sa'ilah), that is, blood that runs; when we slaughter one of them, no blood flows from it. As for the liver and spleen, they are from blood that has reached such a state of purity that it forms an organ of the body, and no organ performing a function in the body is formed from corrupt blood; it must be from pure blood.

The Real, who legislates, takes into account the favorable circumstances of those who are legally responsible (mukallafun). Circumstances and situations may befall them in which they find nothing but carrion, and in such cases they eat out of necessity, to the extent needed to remove harm and hunger. But the Muslim must not fill his stomach with those things. ﴿...But whoever is compelled [by necessity], neither desiring nor transgressing, then indeed your Lord is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (6:145) [Surah al-An'am]. The types of necessity (idtirar) are: that you find nothing lawful to eat, or that lawful food is present but someone compels you to eat this prohibited thing; compulsion falls within necessity, and necessity drives and pushes you to preserve yourself from destruction, so you take of the food enough to sustain yourself so that you do not die of hunger. If Allah has permitted you to eat carrion in a situation where you are likely to die of hunger, then the compulsion to [face] immediate death is more deserving of that permission; for He, glorified is He, is the One who grants the concession (rukhsah) and the One who legislated the concession. This means that it has entered the sphere of legal obligation (taklif), because Allah loves that His concessions be taken just as He loves that His firm commands be observed. And since it has entered the sphere of legal obligation, forgiveness and mercy follow here.

(1) Narrated by Ibn Majah, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi from Ibn 'Umar.

Al-Sha'rawi, the commentary (tafsir) on surah 6, verse 146:

And the Truth (al-Haqq) says after that:

﴿And to those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws; and of oxen and sheep We forbade them their fat, except what their backs or their entrails carry, or what is mixed with bone. That We recompensed them for their rebellion; and indeed We are truthful.﴾

Here the Truth brings the second prohibition, which is a prohibition for refinement and discipline, just as He said earlier: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things which had been made lawful for them...﴾ [Surah al-Nisa' (4): 160].

The "ẓufr" (claw/hoof, a nail-like digit) is what appears when we look at the feet of some animals or birds. There are animals whose toes are split, visibly cloven, with the digits articulated and spread apart from one another; these are not forbidden to them. Another kind has toes that are not separated or spread, such as the camel, the ostrich, the duck and the goose, and these are "dhū ẓufr" (animals with claws). So every animal with claws was forbidden to the Jews. It was forbidden to them not because of any filth or harm in the food itself, but as a discipline for them, because they had wronged by taking what was not their right. Therefore God deprives them of some of what had been lawful to them. A father punishes his son who took his brother's necessity by aggression, so he withholds from him his allowance; the allowance in itself is not forbidden, but the withholding here is for discipline. And the Truth is the One who says: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things which had been made lawful for them, and for their hindering many from the way of God, and their taking usury though they had been forbidden it, and their devouring people's wealth by falsehood...﴾ [Surah al-Nisa' (4): 160–161]. And because they did all that, the prohibition came to them as punishment and discipline: ﴿And to those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws; and of oxen and sheep We forbade them their fat, except what their backs or their entrails carry, or what is mixed with bone. That We recompensed them for their rebellion; and indeed We are truthful.﴾ [Surah al-An'am (6): 146].

When you slaughter an animal, you find some fat on the kidneys, and inside it what they call the "caul" (mindīl al-duhn, the omentum), and likewise the "tail" of a sheep, and when you cut off the head you find a kind of fat in it. The Truth forbade them the fat of oxen and sheep. Likewise "every animal with claws" is forbidden entirely. There is an exception concerning oxen and sheep: ﴿except what their backs or their entrails carry﴾.

That is, He made lawful for them what is upon the back of fat, and made lawful for them the fats carried by the entrails. "Al-ḥawāyā" is the plural of ḥawiyya, ḥāwiya or ḥāwiyā', and it is what is coiled and gathered and wound around (taḥawwā: gathered and curved). In the countryside a woman says of the piece of cloth that she twists and winds and shapes into a round ring, which she places on her head to protect it when carrying things upon it: "I have made a ḥawiyya." Here the ḥawiyya is the large intestine, whose length is so many metres, and from the wisdom of its divine creation we find it coiled around itself; therefore it is called ḥawāyā, and it is what we call the "mesentery" (al-mimbār). Likewise He made lawful for them what is mixed with bone in the legs, the flank, the head and the eye; and likewise He made lawful for them fat mixed with bone, which is the tail-fat, because the tail-fat holds on to the ʿajb al-dhanab, that is, its root, which is the small bone at the base of the tail near the coccyx (ʿuṣʿuṣ). And because He is merciful, He sends down a punishment containing mercy, so He permits some things and forbids others.

The Truth concludes the verse with His saying: ﴿That We recompensed them for their rebellion; and indeed We are truthful.﴾ This prohibition was not an aggression against them, nor a harshness in dealing with them; rather, it was because they rebelled, and the rebel must receive his share of recompense, so that he reflects on what benefit rebellion achieves for him, and what benefit is withheld from him as well. When he compares the two, he may turn away from his rebellion. They had hindered [others] from the way of God, taken usury to increase their wealth, and devoured people's wealth by falsehood; therefore the Truth forbade them some of the lawful. He, glory be to Him, is truthful in every message from Him. We thereby know that the cause of forbidding some of the lawful was their wrongdoing and the sins that proceeded from them, so the prohibition was a punishment for them.

Almighty Allah says after that: ﴿And if they deny you, say: "Your Lord is possessed of vast mercy, but His punishment will not be turned back from the guilty people."﴾

It was to be expected, since they deny you regarding what you have told them from Allah, that Allah would hasten the punishment upon them. But Allah did not hasten the punishment for them, because He is possessed of vast mercy. ﴿Say: "Your Lord is possessed of vast mercy"﴾ (part of verse 147, Surah al-An'am).

But beware of hoping for everlasting mercy; it is only a mercy of postponement. His punishment will not escape you. Here too He addresses them with tenderness, saying: ﴿Say: "Your Lord is possessed of vast mercy"﴾, as if He were saying to them: examine yourselves, be ashamed before Allah, and do not be deceived by the fact that He is your Lord, who created you from nothing and sustained you from non-existence, and took charge of your nurture. For He will not turn back or withhold His might and His punishment from the guilty people among you.

Then He, glory be to Him, says after that: ﴿The idolaters will say: "Had God willed, we would not have associated anything with Him, nor would our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything." Likewise did those before them deny until they tasted Our might. Say: "Have you any knowledge that you can bring forth to us? You follow nothing but conjecture, and you do nothing but guess."﴾ (6:148).

Whenever you read a verse in which "sayaqulu" ("they will say") occurs, know that it contains a secret of the Qur'an's inimitability (i'jaz). What reveals this secret is the opponent, so that you understand how the enemy of God furnishes the proof of God's truthfulness, which shows that he is heedless. Earlier the True One, glory be to Him, said: ﴿The foolish among the people will say...﴾ (2:142). The word "sayaqulu" means that they have not said it yet; the Qur'an informs that they will say it. The Qur'an did not conceal or hide this verse; rather, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited it as Qur'an, read and prayed with it. Had they possessed any reflection, they would have kept silent about the saying, so as to present the speaker of the Qur'an as one who does not utter sound speech, or at least they would have said that he says: "The foolish will say..." and "we are not foolish, so we do not say this." But they utter the foolish saying despite the fact that the verse has preceded them in foretelling what they will say, because the One who informed is God, and no precaution from among God's creation can arise to outdo the truth of God.

They heard the word, and yet they did not fall silent; rather their tongues hastened to it to confirm the Qur'an.

Every person who is extravagant toward himself in not following God's method says: "Our Lord is the One who guides and the One who leads astray," saying this with brazenness and impudence to justify the folly he commits. The extravagant toward themselves will continue to say this, as will the idolaters, and they will attempt to make lawful what God has forbidden. The idolaters brought two claims: a claim in belief and a claim in obligation. In the matter of belief they said: ﴿Had God willed, we would not have associated,﴾ as if they had associated by the will of God. And regarding what they forbade of God's lawful things, they said that they had done so by God's will as well, in order to create a justification for themselves. This statement is not a rational position, for if it were a rational stance it would have been in both directions, good and evil. One of them would say: "Our Lord has decreed evil upon us, God forbid; why then does He punish me?" But this person does not say: "God has decreed good for me." This is what logic would require and demand, but they spoke of evil and remained silent about the good given to them.

Their saying "Had God willed, we would not have associated" is correct in meaning, for if He, glory be to Him, had willed to make all people guided, He would have done so. But He willed to give us choice, and within the framework of this choice nothing falls outside His cosmic will. Rather, disbelief and evil fall outside His legislative will (al-irada al-shar'iyya). We have learned earlier that there is a difference between the cosmic (kawniyya) and the legislative (shar'iyya); the disbelief of the disbeliever and evil are not against God's will or by compulsion from Him, glory be to Him; they occurred and happened through the choice God gave to each human being. The human being is fit to choose between alternatives: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve...﴾ (18:29).

The human being is able to direct the energy God has bestowed upon him, which is apt for good or for evil. Thus the human choice either leads him into faith or turns him toward disbelief. Therefore the True One, speaking of those who claim their disbelief was by God's will, says: ﴿Likewise did those before them deny until they tasted Our might...﴾ (6:148).

Those before them said the same and did the same denial as these do, and there came upon them might and severe punishment from God. Therefore the True One commands Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿...Say: "Have you any knowledge that you can bring forth to us? You follow nothing but conjecture, and you do nothing but guess."﴾ (6:148).

Muhammad (ﷺ) asks them about knowledge by which they might confirm the soundness of what they claim and assert, i.e., whether they have a message from God. The truth is that they have no knowledge or proof; they follow conjecture and guess, meaning that their speech is not clear in indicating what it intends; it is conjecture, guesswork and falsehood.

Therefore He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Say: "To God belongs the conclusive proof. Had He willed, He would have guided you all."﴾ (6:149).

Yes, indeed: had He, glory be to Him, willed, He could have compelled them to guidance. But He did not will that; rather He willed that turning to belief in Him and following the obligations should be a matter within their own choice. Has He not created a kind of creation that does not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and does what they are commanded? Has He not created the whole universe obeying His command? !

﴿Say: "Then to Allah belongs the conclusive proof; so had He willed, He would have guided you all."﴾ [Surah al-An'am]. "Al-hujjah" is the proof that you establish to support your position in debate, and for this reason we call our contracts "hujjah" (documents) for ownership. Or "al-hujjah al-baligha" means the one through which nothing ever penetrates to nullify its purpose.

Then the Almighty says, after that:

﴿Say: "Bring forward your witnesses who testify that Allah has forbidden this." Then if they testify, do not testify along with them, and do not follow the desires of those who denied Our signs and those who do not believe in the Hereafter, and they hold others equal to their Lord.﴾

Since you do not possess knowledge, it is likely that you possess witnesses to what you say. The address "halumma shuhada'akum" (bring forward your witnesses) is addressed to a group. "Halumma" (come, bring) is used in the same form for the singular masculine, singular feminine, dual, masculine or feminine, and for the plural, masculine or feminine. So you say: "Halumma, O Zayd, to me," "Halumma, O Hind, to me," and "Halumma" is also used for a group of males and for a group of females. This is the dialect of the Hijazis. It differs from the dialect of Banu Tamim, who add to it, so they say: "Halumma, O man," "Halumma, O woman," "Halumma (dual)," "Halumma (plural masculine)," and "Halummanna (plural feminine)." The Qur'an was revealed in the language of Quraysh, the Hijazis, and the Almighty says: "Halumma shuhada'akum." That is, bring forward and produce your witnesses that Allah has forbidden this. You have no knowledge, and likewise you have no witnesses for your claim; so if you have witnesses, bring these witnesses.

But what if they bring false witnesses? He, glory be to Him, warns His Messenger and makes clear to him that even if they bring witnesses, beware of believing them, for they are liars.

It is as if Allah wishes to expose the witnesses as well, before those to whom they testify, and to give two matters together: He refutes and nullifies their argument, and exposes the witnesses they brought. It is as though He said: "Bring those who told you this statement," and in that is a disgrace for whoever coached them in these commands.

The Almighty commands His Messenger not to follow those who denied His signs, glory be to Him. The word "ahwa'" (desires) is the plural of "hawa," which is what ferments in the mind and turns a person away from the truth; it is a desire that comes over the mind and makes it deviate from the truth.

They do not only deny Allah's signs; they also do not believe in the Hereafter, because if they believed in the Hereafter they would know that they will be recompensed for this with a recompense fitting their crimes, and if they had considered this matter they would have refrained from following their desires. The Almighty concludes the verse with His noble saying: "and they hold others equal to their Lord."

We understand from the word "ya'diluna" that it comes from "al-'adl" in the sense of equity: when it is said "'adala fi kadha" (he acted justly/deviated in such-and-such), or "'adala bayna fulan wa fulan" (he was equitable between so-and-so and so-and-so), or "'adala fi al-hukm" (he was just in judgment). But "'adala bi kadha" means he made it an equal and a peer. It is used with this meaning in another verse, His saying: "All praise is due to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light; then those who disbelieve hold others equal to their Lord" [6:1].

That is, they make equal to Allah what is not fit to be equal to Him, an equal and a peer to Allah. This is the act of those who ascribe partners to Allah, and likewise of those who do not believe in Allah; one of them swerves away from his Lord, inclines away from Him, turns away from Him, associates others with Him and makes others equal to Him. When pronouncing the word of tawhid, which is "la ilaha illa Allah" (there is no god but Allah), we must take care not to stop at "la ilaha" (there is no god), because that would mean denial and negation of the existence of a god, and that, God forbid, is disbelief. Rather, we must join it to what follows and say "la ilaha illa Allah," or, when we pronounce "la ilaha," our hearts should already be fixed on His oneness and on the attributes of majesty and perfection that are due to Him, exalted is His greatness. The meaning of "la ilaha illa Allah" is that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah, because those worshipped falsely are many, such as idols, stars, jinn, some humans, angels, and others.

The phrase "bi-rabbihim ya'diluna" (they hold others equal to their Lord) indicates that they are people of shirk; likewise whoever denies the existence of Allah swerves from our Lord, inclines away, and turns aside from acknowledging Him as God.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 6, verse 151:

Then the Truth says, after that: ﴿Say: "Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden you: that you associate nothing with Him, and be good to your parents, and do not kill your children because of poverty — We provide for you and for them — and do not approach the indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is hidden, and do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right. This He has enjoined upon you, that you may understand."﴾ (6:151).

We consider this verse and we find no item among the forbidden foods, which are the means by which life is sustained. Rather, we find in it the prohibitions which, if we follow them, would cause us to squander the moral values that are the foundations of spiritual life. These are the foundations of life made of values: ﴿Say: "Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden you."﴾

The Qur'anic expression here takes the word "ta'ala" (come) with a deeper understanding than mere approach. It is as if the Truth says: "Turn to Me with the approach of one who wishes to rise in receiving commands." For you turn to the commands of Allah so that you may be elevated and rise above the lowliness of human legislation. So do not take your laws from the lowliness of human legislation, because the necessary condition in a legislator is that he not be equal to those for whom he legislates, that he not benefit from some of what he legislates, and that he be comprehensive, so that no matter escapes him and nothing is beyond his knowledge. A created legislator legislates only after his intellect has matured and ripened, and he cannot prevent himself from benefiting from the legislation.

The capitalist, for example, legislates to profit, and the Marxist legislates to profit. Each one legislates with a desire in himself, and afterwards the legislations are amended when it becomes clear that they no longer suffice or cover the affairs of life. It is as if the first legislator, because of the deficiency of his knowledge, was unaware of realities which society exposed when the issues emerged. He looked into his law and found nothing covering these issues, so he says: "We will amend the law and make up for what was missed." The meaning of the law's amendment is that there is something he was ignorant of at the time he enacted it.

Therefore, the condition for the one who legislates is that he not be equal to those for whom he legislates, that no matter escape him so that he is not corrected, and that he not benefit from the legislation. This is never found in a human being at all. So the Truth made clear: leave the lowliness of human legislation and rise up to the heavens to take your legislation from them. When Allah calls "Come," its meaning is: rise above the lowliness of the legislation of your humanity to the Highest, so that you take from it your enactments which govern the movement of your lives. He does not benefit from what He has legislated; rather, you are the ones who benefit. And because nothing escapes Him, glory be to Him, and He is the Creator, He is more worthy to legislate for you. ﴿Say: "Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden you."﴾ (part of 6:151).

"Atlu" (I will recite) is from "tilawa," which is reading. ﴿What your Lord has forbidden you﴾: that is, what He has made unlawful, meaning what is prohibited for them to do. I will tell you all the eloquent points, one after another. ﴿That you associate nothing with Him﴾ (part of 6:151).

He, glory be to Him, came with the prohibition of shirk through a linguistic structure that emphasizes for us not to associate anything with Him. When you come to receive orders from one who is over you, you say to him: "Listen to what I forbid you, and follow it." Then you begin the details. Here the Truth has placed as the first item of the prohibitions and forbidden things that we should not associate anything with Him. That is, "I recite to you the prohibition of shirk," so the first of the prohibitions is shirk, and we must affirm the oneness of Allah. Every prohibition of something entails a command for its opposite, and every command for something entails a prohibition of its opposite. Thus every command entails a prohibition, and every prohibition entails a command, so let the commands and prohibitions not be confused for you. Or "upon you" (ʿalaykum) may be taken as disconnected from what precedes it: that is, upon you is leaving shirk, and upon you is goodness to parents, and that you not kill your children, and that you not approach indecencies. That is, adhere to these.

Then He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿and goodness to parents﴾. Here He, glory be to Him, commands the affirmation of goodness to parents. It is a command of obligation, and it entails a prohibition of its opposite, which is disobedience to parents; that is, do not disobey them. Failure to be good to parents falls within what Allah has forbidden. Then He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And do not kill your children because of poverty — We provide for you and for them﴾ (6:151). That is, preserve the lives of your children. If you take it as a prohibition, say it is a prohibition of killing children; if you take it as a command, say: preserve life. As for ﴿because of poverty﴾, that means because of destitution. It is as if they were poor, and as long as poverty exists, a person's preoccupation with his own provision precedes his preoccupation with the provision of one who will come after him. So, O people of poverty, remember that Allah provides for you and provides for those who will come, in addition, who are the children. He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And do not approach the indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is hidden﴾ (6:151).

This is a prohibition of approaching, that is, a prohibition of the circumstances that may lead to the act, not merely a prohibition of the act itself. When Allah willed to forbid Adam and his wife the tree, He said: ﴿And do not approach this tree...﴾ (7:19).

Because approaching may entice to eating. Likewise: ﴿and do not approach the indecencies﴾, that is, do not come to the preliminaries of indecencies by casting a glance or staring at what is forbidden to others. Likewise a woman who displays her adornment; she takes steps toward the preliminaries of indecencies. If she refrains from the preliminaries, she is safe from temptation and slipping. For the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "What is lawful is clear and what is unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters which many people do not know. Whoever avoids doubtful matters has absolved his religion and his honor, and whoever falls into doubtful matters falls into the unlawful, like a shepherd who grazes around the sanctuary, about to fall into it. Surely every king has a sanctuary, and the sanctuary of Allah on earth is what He has forbidden. Surely in the body there is a piece of flesh: if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt; surely it is the heart." (1)

The Truth forbids you: "do not approach," that is, distance yourself from the likelihood that things will seduce you, exactly like "avoid" (ijtanibu). Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿So avoid the abomination of the idols...﴾ (22:30).

And He says: ﴿...and avoid the word of falsehood﴾ (22:30). And here the Exalted says: ﴿and do not approach the indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is hidden﴾.

Everything apparent of indecencies is from the actions of the limbs which commit grave sins, and ﴿what is hidden﴾ is from the actions of the inner secrets, such as rancor, malice and envy.

Glory be to Him continues: ﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right﴾ (6:151). The word "soul" (nafs) — people differ in its meaning, and "soul" is not applied except to the joining of the spirit with matter. The spirit in its essence is good, and matter in its essence is good, glorifying and worshipping. ﴿And there is not a thing but glorifies His praise...﴾ (17:44).

When the spirit joins matter, life arises. So the meaning of killing a soul is to separate the spirit from matter by destroying the structure, and this is other than death, because Allah is the One who causes death. As for the human being in the verse, you will find that intellect gives you balance in decision. The Truth concluded the five things, so whoever destroys its structure kills the soul. The One who bestowed life is Allah, so none takes life except Him. Afterwards, Allah legislates for us that we take life by way of retribution (qisas), or for adultery by a married person, man or woman, or for apostasy. That is a killing by right. But Allah, exalted is He, curses whoever destroys the edifice of Allah without right, and the human being is the edifice of Allah, so do not transgress against him. Therefore Allah commanded us to exact retribution from one who killed a person, so that each one preserves the life of his own self, and when a person preserves every soul, he saves himself and is safe.

Thus the Truth commands that we kill the married adulterer, and the muhsan (married) adulterer applies to male and female, and it is one who has married, entered upon his spouse, and each of them has tasted the other's honey (i.e., consummated). Likewise the apostate. We are keen on freedom of belief; the proof is that we do not kill the original disbeliever for his disbelief. But a person must understand that entering Islam requires that he study it thoroughly and convincingly, and that he know that his life is contingent on not returning from this religion. If he knows that his life is contingent on not returning from this religion, he will not enter it except fully convinced. We protect by choice, so we announce to everyone who approaches Islam and warn him: beware of entering with mere outward words without understanding the meaning of Islam, for if you enter and then afterwards apostatize, you will be killed; and since the thing's price is life, the person must be extremely cautious. In that there is also confidence that a person who seeks out the proofs will be convinced that he has a true God; but we do not kill the original disbeliever.

So, the apostate is mentioned as a safeguard for the firmness of choice. Beware of entering without seeing, for if you enter and then apostatize, you will be killed. Thereby the Truth settles the matter with a necessary settlement: whoever approaches Islam must place all the proofs before himself, and enter only with this intention. In any contract a person seeks to know his obligations and to have them made clear before him. One does not enter the religion with reckless, rash or hasty entry, but must enter with deliberation and vision.

In marriage a person enters with one word and exits with one word as well: "You are divorced." Therefore a woman takes precautions, for since she knows that the continuation of her marriage depends on a word, she must be careful not to place this right except in the hands of one trustworthy with it. When her father says to her: "Listen, you have the right to choose the husband who, if he loves you, honors you, and if he dislikes you, does not wrong you, because with one word from him the marital life ends." So the woman must think about the man trustworthy with this word.

Nevertheless, there is a precaution against heedlessness: a man marries with one word, once, but in divorce there are three stages, as a reserve against heedlessness. A man marries a woman with the words "I have married myself to you" or her guardian marries her to him, and acceptance comes from the husband, and by this the marriage is completed. But in divorce, Allah permitted for the heedlessness and rashness of the man that he divorce once, then take her back without anyone intervening between them, then divorce a second time and take her back; but after the third divorce there is a warning from the Truth: "We have taken precautions for you with a reserve of your heedlessness." But when you want her as a wife again, this will not happen unless she marries someone else, and afterward she may return to you or remain with the one she married. So be very careful about the matter you enter upon and the contract you have undertaken. If this is the case in the marriage contract, what then of apostasy? We kill the apostate, and we do not do that to him before he believes, before he declares his faith and before he enters the sphere of believers; and let him know that if he turns back from Islam he will be killed. Thus Islam makes entry into it difficult, while protecting choice at the same time. He, glory be to Him, continues: ﴿That He has enjoined upon you, that you may understand﴾ (part of 6:151).

"Wasiyya" (injunction) is only for important matters without which life cannot be sound except by performing them; it concerns the mothers of questions that must not be neglected. That is why, when you look at the Prophet (ﷺ), he remained twenty-three years receiving from heaven and conveying to the people of the earth, then came at the Farewell Pilgrimage and concentrated all the principles of the religion in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿That He has enjoined upon you, that you may understand﴾.

"Wassakum" (He has enjoined upon you) is not the same as "shara'a" (He legislated): shara'a brings all legislations with their minor details, while wasiyya comprises the mothers of matters in legislation. Intellect must encompass the matter from its beginning to its end; so if you use your intellect on every prohibited thing, or on every commanded thing in the verse, you will find that intellect gives you balance in decision. The Truth concluded the five things mentioned in this verse with ﴿That He has enjoined upon you, that you may understand﴾. These commands are agreed upon in all the messages and in all the religions, and they are called "the Ten Commandments."

1. Narrated by al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir.

Then the Truth comes, in the next verse, to complete the injunctions, saying:

﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner until he reaches his maturity. Give full measure and weight with justice. We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity. And when you speak, be just, even if it concerns a near relative. And fulfill the covenant of Allah. This He has enjoined upon you that you may remember.  (152)﴾

We know that the orphan is one who has lost his father and has not yet reached the stage of men. This is said of humans. As for the orphan among animals, it is the one who has lost its mother. And the Truth says:

﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner until he reaches his maturity…  (152)﴾ [from verse 152, Surat al-An'am].

Here He, glory be to Him, stipulates that the orphan has property. He did not say, "Do not eat the property of the orphan." Rather, He commanded you not to approach it, even in thought or in consideration, and you must keep away from this matter. If He said, ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan﴾, is this command absolute? No, because He added after that, ﴿except in the best manner﴾, meaning that we should make his property grow in a way that suffices for his living, while the principal remains for him along with an increase. For this reason He said elsewhere: ﴿and provide for them from it﴾ [Surat al-Nisa', 5].

So no one should take the orphan's property and save it, then give him a portion of it each month, so that when he reaches maturity (rushd) he finds the property diminished or lost. Therefore He did not say, "provide for them from it" (minha), but said ﴿provide for them from it﴾ (fiha), meaning: provide for them with a provision arising from it. Their property is thus the container of the provision, and this cannot be achieved except by making it grow for the orphan. We must not deprive the orphan's guardianship of the care of his property by those who are skilled in business management and trustworthy. Sometimes a person is competent in managing work and trustworthy, but his situation does not allow him to bear the burdens and cost of his own livelihood while also managing the orphan's property. Therefore He, glory be to Him, said about this: ﴿And whoever is rich, let him abstain, and whoever is poor, let him take according to what is reasonable﴾ [Surat al-Nisa', 6].

That is, the guardian (al-wasiyy) should dedicate that care to Allah. When he dedicates that care to Allah and takes no wage in return for performing it, he guarantees that if an orphan is found among his descendants until the Day of Resurrection, that orphan will find someone to support him, seeking Allah's reward and voluntarily, with his reward stored up with Allah. The Truth says: ﴿And let those fear who, if they left behind them weak offspring, would be anxious for them. So let them fear Allah and speak words of appropriate justice  (9)﴾ [Surat al-Nisa'].

When the orphan finds someone to care for him, and when society shows compassion toward every orphan within it, and trustworthy people capable of managing their affairs take charge of the affairs of orphans, a person's anxiety about dying and leaving his young children will decrease, because he will find honor and care for the orphan. People fear death because they have small dependents, and they see that society does not care for orphans. But if a person finds the orphan honored, and finds many fathers within the Islamic nation, then if death comes to him, he will be reassured about his children, because they are under the care of society. However, do not wait until society's situation is set right; rather, reform yourself and your conduct toward any orphan. By this you can be assured about your children, for you will find someone to care for them after your death. When the faith-based society cares for every orphan, you will find that people do not become constrained by the decree of Allah concerning His creation, namely that one of them dies and leaves children behind. The example is clear in Surat al-Kahf, concerning the righteous servant and Prophet Musa when they passed by a village: ﴿until, when they came to the people of a town, they asked its people for food  (77)﴾ [Surat al-Kahf].

They did not ask for money to save, but asked for food to satisfy hunger, which is an urgent need. Although they asked the people of the village for food, the people of the village refused to host them. That means it was a village of ignoble people. Despite the righteous servant finding their rejection and their refusal to feed them, when he found a wall, and by his insight knew that the wall wanted to collapse, as if the wall had its own purpose, he set it up straight. Musa, peace be upon him, rebuked him. Musa was logical with himself: he and his companion had asked the people of the village merely for food, and they refused. How could you respond to them by building the wall for them? You should have taken a wage for the building, since they were a people of meanness. This was Musa's statement. But the righteous servant repaid them according to what they deserved, because by building the wall he prevented them from taking the treasure, since if the wall had been left to collapse, the treasure beneath it would have been exposed, and it belonged to two orphans. Thus the righteous servant knew how to train them. Then Allah willed to explain to us that the wall belonged to two orphan boys in the city:

{﴿So your Lord intended that they should reach their maturity and extract their treasure...  (82)﴾ [Surat al-Kahf].

So the extraction of the treasure is linked to the attainment of maturity (rushd). It is as if the righteous servant built the wall as a timed construction, such that it would not collapse except when the two boys reached the level of maturity. The righteous servant built the structure as though he were setting the appointed time, so that the wall would hold only until the moment the two boys reached their full strength, and then the two boys would extract their treasure. After that, He gave the reason for all of this, saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And their father was righteous...  (82)﴾ [Surat al-Kahf].

So it is as if the father's righteousness is what the Truth wanted to show us: how it protected the children's treasure. The righteous servant and Musa come to the mean people of the village, asking for food, and they do not feed them, so the righteous servant builds the timed wall that protects the treasure from the mean. And the Truth says here: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner...  (152)﴾ [Surat al-An'am].

Whoever cannot approach the orphan's property in the best manner should keep away from it.

And so that people do not hold back or avoid caring for the orphan's property out of caution, He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And whoever is rich, let him abstain; and whoever is poor, let him take according to what is reasonable﴾ (part of verse 6, Surat al-Nisa').

The phrase ﴿let him take according to what is reasonable (bil-ma'ruf)﴾ means he should never hoard or save any of it, but should eat only what stops hunger and clothe himself with what covers his body. We know that the orphan's mind has not yet matured, and likewise the adult who is foolish (safih) is also unable to manage his affairs. Therefore the Truth, in His eloquent expression in which the wording conveys wide meanings, said: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property...  (part of verse 5, Surat al-Nisa')﴾.

The Truth placed the property of the foolish person in the same rank as the property of the guardian (wali), because the foolish person does not respect his own ownership and may squander it. But the property returns to this person when his foolishness departs, and the Truth says: ﴿But if you perceive in them maturity of judgment, then release their property to them  (part of verse 6, Surat al-Nisa')﴾.

This is a wonderful Qur'anic expression that encourages people not to let the foolish squander their wealth, which would be a loss to the whole society. As long as he is in foolishness, regard the property as though it were yours, and be trustworthy with it as you would be with your own property. When you see and find his maturity, and are reassured of it, the Truth commands you to return his property to him. Returning to the orphan, here the Truth says: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner﴾.

This applies if he has property. What about the orphan who has no property? Here the injunction is even stronger. On the authority of Sahl ibn Sa'd, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I and the one who cares for an orphan are like this," and he pointed with his index and middle fingers and spread them apart. (1)

And on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The one who strives for the widow and the needy is like the one who fights in the cause of Allah, and like one who fasts by day and stands in prayer by night." (2)

Take care, and make the stroking of the orphan's head purely for Allah. It is possible that the orphan has a beautiful mother, and the guardian wants to get close to her through the child. Beware of that, for besides displeasing and angering Allah, it is baseness, meanness, and vileness. ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner until he reaches his maturity…  (152)﴾ [Surat al-An'am].

Allah, glory be to Him, did not say "bil-allati hiya hasanah" (in a good manner), but said ﴿bil-allati hiya ahsan﴾ (in the best manner), to intensify the care for the orphan's property until he reaches his maturity (ashudd). Reaching ashudd means that the orphan has acquired an independent selfhood. And what is the criterion for independent selfhood? That he becomes capable of begetting someone like himself, and this is the standard of maturity. He is like fruit when it ripens: the seed within it becomes fit to be planted in the ground to become a tree. If you pluck fruit before it ripens, you will not find its taste sweet, and you will not enjoy its flavor until the seed is complete and ripe.

The "ashudd" means that a person becomes capable of begetting someone like himself, which is what we call puberty (al-bulugh). He also becomes capable of managing property well and everything else. He continues, glory be to Him: ﴿And give full measure and weight with justice  (part of verse 152, Surat al-An'am)﴾.

The kayl (measure) is the standard for what is measured by volume, and the mawazin (scales) are the standards for what is measured by density. So there is a standard for volume and a standard for density. The standard for volume is the measure (kayl), and the standard for density is weight. There are also fair estimates in measurement, for example for cloth, where the standard is the meter. So everything is according to its kind, and if you want to weigh something, there must be justice (qist), that is, fairness.

This matter is difficult to achieve, and therefore scales differ according to the preciousness of things. When we weigh beans, lentils, potatoes, or taro, we weigh them on a large scale, because the margin of the scale may be around a kilogram, so the matter is acceptable in that case. When we weigh things that are somewhat more valuable, we use a precise scale. If the thing being weighed is gold, we surround the scale with glass walls, because a gust of air may decrease or increase the weight.

We try to prevent the influence of air currents on us. When we weigh chemicals, we use a scale that works by the atom. So everything weighed takes the degree of precision of its scale according to its value and sensitivity, because achieving justice in weighing is a difficult matter, and the same is true of measuring. When a person measures a measure, he holds the vessel and shakes it so that the measure comes out precise and level. If he wants to abandon his conscience and take more than his right, he fills the measure beyond its capacity and holds the excess with his hand so that it does not spill. The Lord says: ﴿Woe to those who give less [in measure or weight]. Who, when they take a measure from people, take it in full. But when they give by measure or weight to others, they cause loss  (1-3)﴾ [Surat al-Mutaffifin].

When he takes the measure, he takes it in full, and when he cheats (tatfif), he adds to what he will receive as payment; and when he sells, he reduces the measure or weight in order to take a price greater than the price of what he weighs or measures. Trade is generally between two parties, and some pedants say: How can the Truth say ﴿Woe to those who give less﴾ when cheating in any matter occurs by increase, not by decrease? We say: Notice that the speaker is Allah, and cheating increases one party and decreases the other, and every transaction between two people involves buying and selling. If one wants to make the loss fall on one party and to take the full amount for himself, then he is a cheat (mutaffif).

Therefore the precision of the Qur'anic expression comes from our Lord: ﴿And give full measure and weight with justice; We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity  (152)﴾ [Surat al-An'am].

The Truth said this because He knows that measuring and weighing with justice is a matter that is hard to attain. Because of His vast mercy in legislating for us, the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, did not make the scope of capacity a matter that could be controlled by things outside capacity. In regulating the measure and the scale, He said: ﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾, because the measure and the scale are two instruments that…
